subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON PLANS TO MAINTAIN NATIONAL UNITY-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 to move a motion of urgent and pressing necessity. The Minister of National Health and Welfare has claimed in an interview that the separatists in Quebec voted Liberal in the by-elections two days ago. This clearly implies that the separatist voter in Quebec has decided that the quickest way to achieve his aims of breaking up the country is to keep the federal Liberals in power in Ottawa. Therefore, 1 move, seconded by the hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. Holmes):
That the Prime Minister state on motions what new initiatives he plans to take in view of this interesting development.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO PROHIBIT ESTABLISHMENT OF FACILITIES FOR PRODUCTION OF PLUTONIUM-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity under the provisions of Standing Order 43, which arises out of information made available yesterday that AECL, a federal Crown corporation, has established a co-ordinating committee with Ontario Hydro in order to develop detailed plans to establish a nuclear energy facility for the production of plutonium, a substance extremely dangerous both to produce and to maintain. It is precisely this substance with its dangerous possibilities that President Carter in the United States recently decided to ban from production, concluding that such critically radioactive fuel could lead to devastation on a massive scale should a major nuclear accident occur. Grave doubts have also been raised on precisely this matter by the government of the
United Kingdom. I therefore, move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources take immediate action to prohibit AECL from continuing with its plans with Ontario Hydro to establish a nuclear energy facility for the production of plutonium.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO PROHIBIT ESTABLISHMENT OF FACILITIES FOR PRODUCTION OF PLUTONIUM-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, I ask for the unanimous consent of the House to move an important motion of pressing necessity.
Considering that last Sunday evening the English network of the CBC on its program News Magazine dealt with the by-elections during which the Social Credit Party of Canada was completely ignored while the leaders of the other three federal political parties were introduced, considering that last Tuesday evening the French network of the CBC did likewise, interviewing the leaders of the other three parties, two of which did not even have a single member elected and wilfully refraining from interviewing the leader of my party, who was in the Temiscamingue constituency with the new Social Credit member, Mr. Gilles Caouette, and considering that such a situation is not new but well established, 1 move, seconded by the hon. member for Abitibi (Mr. Laprise):
That the House of Commons severely criticize the CBC for its discrimination against the Social Credit Party of Canada.

speechtext:

[Mr. Speaker.)
folly in my view to abolish controls before the general election". Would the Prime Minister indicate to the House whether this quotation accurately represents his views?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM DATE ON WHICH CONTROLS ABOLISHED
speechtext: Well, Mr. Speaker, accurately with a slight hyperbole introduced into the language. speechtext: Would the Prime Minister indicate what he feels is the present state of the voluntary agreement that he may be seeking so far as labour and business are concerned? Is there progress? Can the Prime Minister announce that in fact there will be such an agreement in the near future?

subtopic: REQUEST FOR PROGRESS REPORT ON VOLUNTARY AGREEMENT ON RESTRAINT BY BUSINESS AND LABOUR

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, of course, the president was speaking in his personal capacity when he stated his opinion about the views of the government. subsubtopic: REASON FOR FAILURE OF DEPARTMENT TO MAKE A FAIR PERCENTAGE OF PURCHASES IN ATLANTIC REGION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Supply and Services. It relates to the procurement policies of the Department of Supply and Services. Although the Atlantic region contains 9.5 per cent of Canadas population, of the $1 billion spent on commercial supply by the minister's department only 6.3 per cent went to the region and of the $1.9 billion spent on science and engineering procurement only 2 per cent went to benefit Atlantic Canadian industry. Since these percentages, which underline the minister's negligence with respect to regional development needs-they are well below any proportion based on relative population and in one case involve a reduction by as much as 50 per cent compared with expenditure in the previous year- can the minister explain why he is following policies which, in effect, cause greater regional disparity in the Atlantic region and which seem to fly in the face of action taken both by his colleague, the Minister for Regional Economic Expansion and of the government's overall commitment?

subsubtopic: MR. CROSBIE-TERRA NOVA GOLF COURSE-RULING BY MR SPEAKER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege.
I shall be very brief. I rise on a question of privilege today because I feel that my rights and privileges were not respected by a Crown corporation, namely the Canadian National. Let me explain myself.
Last Friday, May 20, I took the CN train for Montreal at 4.30 p.m. I was sitting with the son-in-law and daughter of the hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Rondeau), and behind me sat the hon. member for Lachine-Lakeshore (Mr. Blaker), all of whom can bear witness to the following facts. When the train controller went by asking for tickets as usual, 1 showed him my MP identification card with a photo of myself instead of the official green card issued to MPs bearing the signature of the clerk of the House of Commons which according to the law entitles all hon. members to travel free of charge on all railways in Canada. On that official card one can read that, under the law, the hon. member can travel on all trains in Canada. That card certifies only that I am a member of parliament. Yet, my MP identification card also testifies to the fact that 1 am a member of parliament. The controller refused to accept my official MP card and unfortunately a heated argument ensued. There were other people around which of course annoyed me tremendously. The controller insisted on my buying a ticket, which I refused to do. In addition, Mr. Speaker, I made an attempt to speak English to him-and this I say without wanting to discriminate against anyone- because he did not speak a word of French. It is only later that he called for the help of a French-speaking colleague of his.
In a word, therefore, I feel frustrated in a right conferred upon me under legislation as regards travel by train and furthermore this controller did not speak French, whereas the Official Languages Act states that all services provided by government agencies must be offered in the citizen's language. I hardly think the train would get off the track should someone aboard speak French.
Privilege-Mr. Lavoie
Sometime ago, Mr. Speaker, I happened to be travelling along with the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. Joyal). He did not have this green pass and yet he identified himself with the same card as I and nothing happened. Everything was in order. I have checked with Mr. Smith of the Canadian National who was in a way very negative in his answer. I have also contacted the Clerk of the House who told me I was right to present this card. Therefore, I ask the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) to solve this problem concerning the Montreal-Ottawa or Ottawa-Montreal line and in addition I want the Canadian National authorities to make formal apologies in order to mitigate the prejudice that was done to me under those circumstances without, however, taking any corrective action against this controller. I had to draw the House's attention to this unfortunate incident which could happen to any one of us in this Chamber and I think it is important that we may avail ourselves of our privileges on those trains which are run by a Crown agency.

Second, the hon. member draws our attention to the fact that there is no staff member, no bilingual controller, who can speak French or communicate in either of the two official languages on a train run by a Crown corporation. Those are important issues. I will inquire into the circumstances.

speechtext: Cossitt wouldn't let us answer them.

May 26, 1977

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, hon. members opposite may not have been keeping track of the progress of business in this House, but it is interesting to note that for the past several weeks the rate of answering questions in this House has been running well in excess of 70 per cent. speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prince Albert) moved:
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GRAIN HANDLING AND TRANSPORTATION
speechtext:
That this House agrees in principle with the recommendations of the Hall Commission on Grain Handling and Transportation.
He said: Mr. Speaker . ..

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GRAIN HANDLING AND TRANSPORTATION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GRAIN HANDLING AND TRANSPORTATION
speechtext: I am always pleased to hear applause from the government side of the House, particularly from ministers of the Crown. I think it was Walpole who said, "They ring bells now, but they wring hands later".

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GRAIN HANDLING AND TRANSPORTATION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GRAIN HANDLING AND TRANSPORTATION
speechtext:
Speaking on this resolution, 1 cannot cover very much ground because of the limitation of time. 1 will simply begin by referring to one or two highlights of the Hall report. One of them is the question of abandonment, and I say immediately that as far as that is concerned, having examined some of the representations made, 1 hope that in areas on the prairies which have been pioneer settlements, the removal of the rails from those areas and the creation of desert towns and villages will be proceeded with carefully. I will deal with the construction of an Arctic railway a little later.
The Hall Commission report recommends the retention of the Crowsnest, or statutory rates for hauling grain, with the difference between those rates and the actual cost of transporting grain to be paid directly to the railways by the federal government. The report recommends assistance for Churchill, it suggests changes in connection with freight rates and recommends the use of CPR facilities in order to increase the amount of wheat shipped that way. Those references are general.
As far as the Hall commission is concerned, it constituted a blow to the solar plexus of the government, if not lower, and some of the observations made by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), subsequently diluted in order to meet the exigencies of criticism, indicated that he was greatly surprised at the nature thereof. Indeed, it reminded me of an occasion in earlier days when there were Progressive members from western Canada-"Progressive" being the name of the party-and Prime Minister King had promised a degree of free trade never before seen or felt. One member was greatly exercised over the fact that there was no inclusion of any free trade items and, being a man of classical knowledge and wisdom, said, "Mr. Speaker, when Pandora's box was opened, out stepped the Trojan horse." In this case, as far as the government is concerned and judging from the reaction of the Minister of Transport, there are several Trojan horses in the Hall Commission report. It is a remarkable document. 1 am glad to say it was my recommendation that made Mr. Hall a Superior
80016-37V2

May 26, 1977
Hall Commission Report
Court judge and at the same time set him up as a commissioner of repute.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GRAIN HANDLING AND TRANSPORTATION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GRAIN HANDLING AND TRANSPORTATION
speechtext:
What does the report do? It buries the government's concept of the user-pay philosophy of the minister. User-pay, presented by the minister as a rationalization of transportation services, was little more than a transparent attempt, in the opinion of many, to reduce the benefit to farmers of western Canada under the Crowsnest pass rates.
It is with these matters that I am going to deal at some length. I am very happy to see here today, following a crusade to the Pelly constituency where a by-election is going on and where drought has not affected the area, the new Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Horner). 1 am happy to see him here. Then there is the Minister of Transport. I understand he is in charge of political organization there, which leads everyone to hope that the Liberals will come in third.
As far as the royal commission report is concerned, covering as it does only the western provinces and the north, I think a commission should be set up now to do justice to the maritimes and to go into the whole problem of transportation, freight rates, etc. Otherwise, the provinces by the sea will continue to be denied, as they have been under this government, a reasonable degree of economic equality.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GRAIN HANDLING AND TRANSPORTATION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GRAIN HANDLING AND TRANSPORTATION
speechtext:
One of those who has constantly pressed for action in this regard is the hon. member for Cumberland-Colchester North (Mr. Coates). During my period of administration as prime minister tremendous changes took place in the maritimes. I recall some of the approbation given to what we did by the Minister without Portfolio before he occupied that distinguished portfolio.
Now, sir, I shall immediately start on the subject of the Crowsnest pass report. I am glad to see the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Goodale) here. A moment ago I thought he was going into flight. He put his arms out like the beginning of a flight into fancy when he endeavoured to explain the delays in answering questions which has become virtually beyond anything that has ever been seen in this House.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GRAIN HANDLING AND TRANSPORTATION
speechtext: Shame.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GRAIN HANDLING AND TRANSPORTATION
speechtext: I find him an interesting individual, Mr. Speaker. He sits by his mentor and philosopher today, and he is being misled. I find it very interesting that he has become the "No, no" man of parliament. There he sits; he does not hear what the motions are that come before the House under Standing Order 43, but he invariably says "No".

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GRAIN HANDLING AND TRANSPORTATION
speechtext: I listen very carefully.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GRAIN HANDLING AND TRANSPORTATION
speechtext:
I have some very good examples in regard to which he has been identified. I have watched him with that interest one applies to an individual who apparently does not

want to speak out loudly but simply says very low, sotto voce, "No".

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GRAIN HANDLING AND TRANSPORTATION
speechtext: But very effectively.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GRAIN HANDLING AND TRANSPORTATION
speechtext:
I suggest if he is getting his training from the Minister of Transport as to parliament, he ought to change his mentor. On May 18 the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Hnatyshyn) moved the following motion under Standing Order 43:
That in view of the statement made on national television yesterday by a member of the federal cabinet that the cabinet should accept the recommendation of the Hall commission in connection with the retention of the statutory Crowsnest pass rates, this House direct the Prime Minister to make a statement on motions forthwith outlining the government's commitment to this recommendation of the Hall commission.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GRAIN HANDLING AND TRANSPORTATION
speechtext: It does not say that in the record.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GRAIN HANDLING AND TRANSPORTATION
speechtext: It is very obvious that I have penetrated the epidermis of the hon. gentleman. The truth hurts. Now 1 go on to the next one.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GRAIN HANDLING AND TRANSPORTATION
speechtext: Your fantasy is amazing.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GRAIN HANDLING AND TRANSPORTATION

speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GRAIN HANDLING AND TRANSPORTATION

May 26, 1977

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GRAIN HANDLING AND TRANSPORTATION

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GRAIN HANDLING AND TRANSPORTATION
speechtext:
Ralph Goodale again said "No".
1 want the hon. member's constituents to know what his attitude is in parliament. He has become the puppet of the Minister of Transport. There are other examples, and if he would like to hear them 1 would be glad to indicate them to him. No matter what comes up that would be of benefit to agriculture in Canada, the hon. member says "No".

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GRAIN HANDLING AND TRANSPORTATION
speechtext: Nonsense.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GRAIN HANDLING AND TRANSPORTATION
speechtext: Shame.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GRAIN HANDLING AND TRANSPORTATION
speechtext:
1 suggest it would be simpler if he installed a gramophone in this House saying "No, no, no", and save his larynx. 1 have watched him day after day. He is an intelligent fellow, as you must admit. But he shows little intelligence when he prevents the House of Commons discussing questions of prime importance to western farmers. 1 have said over and over again that this government opposes the Crowsnest rates. The minister denies this, in an uncertain way. Let me read some of his observations, equivocations, qualifications and the like. On May 18 he was asked a question in the House concerning this matter. He replied, as reported at page 5758 of Hansard'.
-my initial reaction ... is very favourable indeed. It seems to me to make a good deal of sense and to have a great deal of potential... While some people raised an idea like that in various discussions before the Hall commission report, it does not really come upon the prairies as a new idea in its totality-
That is a good word, "totality". I continue:
-and I would like to hear from the representatives of farm organizations-
Time and again the minister has played havoc with those who have endeavoured to stand in support of the Crowsnest rates. I remember when Conservatives opposed them. In the election of 1925 Right Hon. Arthur Meighen said freight rates should not be fixed by statute. I took strong objection. He was defeated. The Liberal party said that the magna carta of the western farmer could not be changed without creating serious
Hall Commission Report
fissures in confederation. 1 go on quoting from Hansard. On page 5759 the following exchange is reported:

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GRAIN HANDLING AND TRANSPORTATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have one further supplementary question. How does the minister reconcile his first answer with his answer to my second question, because it is a complete distortion of the facts?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GRAIN HANDLING AND TRANSPORTATION
speechtext:
No it is not, Mr. Speaker. I indicated quite clearly that I have no policy which would affect the Crowsnest rate . . . What I said in my second answer is that I have been discussing this with people in the west, and I am certainly receptive to conclusions in the west that some different form of distributing the benefit may in fact be advantageous to the west.
There are loopholes large enough in the minister's position for-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GRAIN HANDLING AND TRANSPORTATION
speechtext: A horse and wagon?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GRAIN HANDLING AND TRANSPORTATION
speechtext: -an aircraft to go through. All the way along the minister has been playing with facts and endeavouring to lead people to think he has taken a stand not against those particular rates. One could go on almost indefinitely in this regard. If the minister denies it, 1 call as a witness one whom, ever since he was a little boy, the minister regarded as a friend. I refer to the Minister without Portfolio.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GRAIN HANDLING AND TRANSPORTATION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GRAIN HANDLING AND TRANSPORTATION
speechtext: He was younger on September 1, 1966, when he said, as reported at page 7997 of Hansard'. "It appears that the government wants to ruin the Crowsnest pass rates." That was an interesting and obvious observation.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GRAIN HANDLING AND TRANSPORTATION
speechtext: Oh, Jack!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GRAIN HANDLING AND TRANSPORTATION
speechtext:
I do not want to be unfair, but 1 call the Minister without Portfolio as my chief witness. When the credibility of the Minister of Transport comes into question, I am prepared to accept his views. 1 now quote a report carried in the Globe and Mail of November 27, 1976, as follows:
Mr. Horner accused Mr. Lang of "careless disregard of the public trust as Minister of Transport."
Has there been any reformation? Has the minister changed? Is he a chameleon? I could quote further passages. Has the minister without transport-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GRAIN HANDLING AND TRANSPORTATION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GRAIN HANDLING AND TRANSPORTATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, that was a lapsus linguae, but most prophetic. You should have seen the Minister of Transport as I saw him here in all his attractiveness and sartorial perfection. But I never saw the minister look more disturbed than when the Minister without Portfolio crossed to that side of the House. He has recovered now. They are getting together. Nonetheless, as the Ukrainian proverb says, "What is written cannot be drawn out, not even by a team of horses".

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GRAIN HANDLING AND TRANSPORTATION
speechtext: Isn't it Polish?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GRAIN HANDLING AND TRANSPORTATION
speechtext:
The Minister without Portfolio said the Canadian dollar had slipped below the level of the United States dollar because the Liberal government had deliberately held interest rates four percentage points above those in the

May 26, 1977
Hall Commission Report
United States. They are still higher now. Who changed-the minister or the government? He went on to make one of his kinder statements, saying the government is guilty of gross mismanagement of the economy. High unemployment rates in central and eastern Canada are proof of government bungling. He is reported to have said that in November last, and conditions are worse now. I look forward to the explanation of the Minister without Portfolio. I understand he intends to speak. I hope I can stay, although I must leave by an early flight. I do not have the same facilities as the Minister of Transport.
I could go on. 1 do not intend to say anything of a critical nature. What did the Minister of Transport say when the Hall Commission report came out? The Saskatoon Star-Phoenix called it a sensible report. That newspaper has always shown a high regard for the minister. In its issue of Wednesday, May 18, it said this:
In fact, so far it is the singular exclusion of the Minister of Transport from the collective endorsement that inspires speculation on the future of the Hall report.
Why was the minister silent? He is not noted for his silence. He has an unusual capacity for language and articulation, but remained silent. The editorial goes on to say:
Surely Ottawa will notice a golden opportunity to make friends in the west, and thereby strengthen the unity of Canada.
The Hall report's lack of equivocation on the statutory Crowsnest pass freight rates, and the recommendation to extend them to processed grain products and livestock has settled fears once raised by Mr. Lang with his calls for reassessment.
He raised this in the House the other day. I have already read that portion which says, "We have to look into the cost." Did he look into the cost when his aircraft ran up a $750,000 bill in three years? Did he consider cost then? Mr. Speaker, there is no greater repentance than that of the unrepentant. Has the minister changed? I await his answer. But everywhere one notes the same equivocation in which he indulged the other day in this House. He went on to say he had been misreported-everybody out of step but the hon. gentleman- in the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix by Canadian Press. I heard the minister over the radio. Despite any difficulties 1 might have with hearing, it was very clear he was equivocating about this question, at the same time saying that anyone who contends he is against the rates is not telling the truth. However, he did not say he was for them clearly, definitely and finally. It was always subject to equivocation.
1 have high regard for the minister. I remember at one time 1 criticized him. I asked, "What does he know about marketing wheat?" I was right. Today we have 750 million bushels piled up higher than the pyramids that existed when we came into power in 1957. Outside the House the minister made the statement, "Apparently the right hon. member does not know I was born on a farm, almost in the centre of a wheat field." 1 would point out to him that so were gophers.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GRAIN HANDLING AND TRANSPORTATION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GRAIN HANDLING AND TRANSPORTATION
speechtext: We do not want any more equivocation. We want a definite, clear and undiluted statement that there is going to be no tinkering with the Crowsnest pass rates. That is all we ask for.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GRAIN HANDLING AND TRANSPORTATION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GRAIN HANDLING AND TRANSPORTATION
speechtext: I do know why the minister decided to bring about this "at and east" rate. It would have cost the western farmer six cents a bushel more to transport his wheat at Atlantic ports. Why would you expect a minister representing the province of Saskatchewan to be in favour of that? He stood; he fought; he said, "This rock shall move as soon as I." The Conservative party also stood; they fought, and they got a withdrawal. The hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankow-ski) fought on and on.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GRAIN HANDLING AND TRANSPORTATION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GRAIN HANDLING AND TRANSPORTATION
speechtext:
Finally, the minister capitulated. Why did he want to bring in new freight rates for the Welland canal, again hooking the western farmer? He thought he could do it unilaterally. However, the United States made it perfectly clear to him they would not stand for that. The only thing that saved the western farmer from that extra tariff, and that is what I call it, on western production was the fact that the United States refused to follow. It decided it would give further consideration to the matter. I have covered this matter as succinctly as I can. I simply ask the minister to stand and say, "All my past is forgotten. I am for the Crowsnest pass rates now, without evasion, equivocation or mental reservation whatever." When he does that, I will believe him, because he will not be able to do anything else if he gives that undertaking.
We now come to another matter. The Hall commission rather disturbed the government in connection with its recommendation of a railroad into the north. I have been dealing with that matter for several years. I am not going to quote what I have said on previous occasions. On February 24, 1973, 1 dealt at length with the benefits that would flow from a railroad built into the north. Beside opening the north, it would deny all those dangers that follow the building of a pipeline. It would create employment for thousands of Canadians.
The Hall commission described the plan it had in mind for opening the north as the "northern dream". I remember when I uttered the expression of the "northern dream". It was ridiculed by the Liberal party. Then when it turned out all right, those who condemned it became its projectors. They laughed at the idea of a railroad to Great Slave Lake and Pine Point. They said it would be two streaks of rust and a roadbed going nowhere. Mr. Pearson said the Conservatives were going to build highways and railways from igloo to igloo. That shows how up to date the Liberal party was, because they said the same thing in 1873 when Macdonald had his dream-only then they said "from wigwam to wigwam". The philosophy is still there.
I raised this question the other day. Somebody in the press said I must have known in advance that it would be in the Hall
May 26, 1977

report. I had no indication, but I knew the report was coming in so I raised the question in the House. I endeavoured to bring the matter before the House in a motion on May 10, and I quote:
In view of the strong views expressed by the hon. Mr. Justice Berger in connection with a gas pipeline from the Yukon and that a railroad was commended and approved by the Canadian Institute of Guided Ground Transport in 1972 following an engineering, economic and environmental feasibility study of a railroad to carry Arctic oil and liquefied natural gas to markets in central Canada, and as the institute agreed with an earlier preliminary analysis which concluded that a railway is technically and operationally feasible and appeared to be financially attractive, with unanimous consent of the House, I would move:
That a committee of the House be set up to examine this question without delay, as the conclusion of the Canadian Institute was that 360 locomotive units and 1 1,000 tank cars of 94 ton capacity with 20 trains per day could move the necessary requirements of oil and gas.
Furthermore, having regard to the unemployment situation, the report agreed that such a railroad would require 5,000 workers to build over a 516 year period, and it would employ, on completion, some 4,600 people in the Yukon and Northwest Territories, and there would be very little disruption to the environment.
You, Mr. Speaker, asked whether there was unanimous consent, and that voice which went unrecognized said "No." Why? What was the reason for that? All I have to say in that regard is that this parliament is being emasculated by the kind of thing that we witness here day after day. Regardless of whether a motion is in keeping with the kind of Canada we want to bring about, that silent "No" denies parliament the right to speak.

Mr. Speaker, first of all I would like to say I am very pleased to follow our senior colleague from Saskatchewan, the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) and I want to congratulate him on the statesmanlike way in which he dispatched the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Goodale). Not only did he dispatch the hon. member for Assiniboia, whom he scared out of the House, while the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) is still here, but he also scared out of the House the Minister without Portfolio from Alberta (Mr. Horner).

May 26, 1977
Hall Commission Report
I am happy to have the opportunity to take part in this debate initiated by the right hon. member for Prince Albert. 1 support in general the principles of the Hall Report. 1 think the report was a very good one. In style, it is similar to the Berger report, also referred to by the right hon. gentleman. In the course of his study, Mr. Hall took his commission into about 77 different communities on the prairies. He talked to about 15,000 people who attended the hearings. Many of us, as members of parliament, myself included, made presentations to the Hall commission. A large number of community leaders, farm groups, and so on, presented their briefs to the commission. I hope the government acts, and acts quickly, on the recommendations in the report because some of those recommendations are vital to small towns and villages across the prairies.
The question might be asked: Why was the Hall commission appointed in the first place? I want to go back over history and consider what motivated the government to appoint the commission a couple of years ago. First, there was the question of the future of some 6,300 miles of railway across the prairies. The government had decided that 12,450 miles of railway on the prairies would form what they called a basic network guaranteed until the year 2000. Then they classified another 6,300 miles as "B railways", on which operations were frozen until January 1, 1975, following the WEOC conference in Alberta. Then, after the commission was appointed, the freeze was extended until June 30 of this year.
The commission was also to study the port utilization question, grain rates, economic development on the prairies, agricultural processing and the Arctic railway, something which was also referred to by the right hon. member for Prince Albert. Let us consider the situation which existed on the prairies and which led to the setting up of the commission in the first place. Those of us who come from the prairies know that over the last few years there has been an increase in what is known as "western alienation". People are more than ever concerned as to whether or not the west is playing its full role in Canada and getting its full share from this great country. One of the major causes of complaint on the prairies is the transportation system and the way it is set up to benefit, not the people of the prairies, but in the main the vested interests which live in what is called the "golden horseshoe" of southern Ontario.
Many people in the west are also very upset that much of our raw material is shipped to central Canada for processing and we, in turn, have to import the finished products back to the prairies, losing economic opportunity and potential jobs for our people. Another area of great concern to us is the tariff structure in Canada. We seem to see a generous attitude taken toward manufacturing in this country. The average manufacturing tariff is around 30 per cent. Most of the manufacturing, of course, takes place in central Canada. The tariff on agricultural goods is about one half of 1 per cent. This, again, appears to be discriminatory toward those who live on the prairies. People from my area who go down to Minnesota or North Dakota ask me why they are able to buy manufactured goods
[Mr. Nystrom.J
so cheaply just a few miles south of the border. The answer is that although we give industries primarily in southern Ontario tariff protection, our farm goods produced by our own people have no tariff protection whatever.
I come now to the question of rail line abandonment. I have already said that possibly 6,300 miles of rail line are going to be abandoned on the prairies. A study has just been released by the University of Regina, commissioned by the government of Saskatchewan, of the economic and social impact of the abandonment of rail lines on the prairies. This study, which was released to the public on Thursday, May 12 last, found that 47 per cent of businesses and 28 per cent of the population will leave towns and villages along rail lines which will be abandoned. This study focused on 26 communities with a population of more than 100 people, selected from 374 centres served by rail lines which the government is considering abandoning. The Hall commission is as important to people on the prairies as is the Berger inquiry to the people of northern Canada, and it is why the Hall report must be taken seriously by the government.
People in my area also have a great deal of concern about some of the proposals to build huge inland terminals and to close down country elevators which serve small towns in my own province and my neighbouring province. They are also concerned about statements, made by the Minister of Transport-my right hon. friend from Prince Albert put it very well this afternoon-to the effect that the government is equivocating on the Crow rates, that it is not coming out squarely in favour of retaining the Crow rates but saying that farmers should instead receive the benefits of the Crow rates in some other way. I want to know, in what other way. 1 want to know whether the minister will tell us in a straightforward manner that he is standing firmly behind the Crow rates and will not change them as recommended in the Hall commission report.
My constituents are also concerned about the user-pay philosophy of the Minister of Transport. This is a concept which would hurt people on the prairies. If it were applied literally, it would mean that farmers and businessmen on the prairies would pay the full cost of transporting their goods and materials across this country. That in itself would discriminate against regions like the prairies, the north and the maritimes which are a long way from the markets of this country.
These are the circumstances which led to the Hall commission inquiry on the prairies and to the establishment of a study which I think is one of the most worthwhile we have seen in a long while. A number of recommendations were made which I support in principle and which I believe should be acted upon as quickly as possible. Let me take them one by one. First is the very important question of rail line abandonment. The Commission took a look at the 6,300 miles of B rail lines across the prairies which were going to be abandoned. They held hearings across the prairies and then recommended that some 1,800 miles be incorporated into the basic rail network, the existence of which will be guaranteed until at least the
May 26, 1977

year 2000. That is a good recommendation, Mr. Speaker, one that the minister should immediately agree to when he takes the floor in about 15 minutes' time. By doing so he will give towns, villages and delivery points along those railways some certainty of their future, and thus enable them to plan their communities and economies in the years ahead.
The report also found that some 2,165 miles of line should be abandoned between June 30 of this year and 1981. We all agree that some rail lines must be abandoned. In fact, some 600 miles of line have not been used for the last two years. However, I suggest the Minister of Transport take another look at some of the proposed abandonments. I can think of 200 or 300 miles of line which perhaps should not be abandoned. For example, in my own riding, Jedburgh and Colmer, both little places, deliver a fair amount of grain and depend on the railways. Perhaps they should be given a second chance and the railroad retained.
The third recommendation in regard to rail line abandonment is to put 2,340 miles of rail lines under the authority of a new Crown corporation to be known as the prairie rail authority. This is a new idea. The Hall commission says it is not really sure that these lines should be abandoned and that 2,300 miles of rail line should be examined very thoroughly by a new federal Crown corporation and retained until the year 1990. By that time a decision must be made whether to abandon or retain them.
In some ways, Mr. Speaker, I think that is very unfortunate, because uncertainty will continue to exist in many communities along those rail lines. There will be uncertainty as to whether or not the Wheat Pool and other grain elevators should upgrade their facilities or build new elevators. Just the other day the president of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool announced that one new elevator planned for a certain town would not now be built. After all, what is the use of building an elevator if the rail line is abandoned in 12 years' time? What is the point of setting me a new business in a town or village on the rail line if the line is to be abandoned? Therefore, if the government accepts this recommendation they will, in effect, be telling a whole series of towns with significant populations that they will face long-term uncertainty.
In face of this de facto uncertainty over a long period, Mr. Speaker, the rail lines will indeed be abandoned. If the elevator companies do not upgrade their facilities, if businessmen do not expand, and new plants are not set up owing to this uncertainty as to the existence of the railway after 1990, then the CTC, the government, or the prairies rail authority, or whichever body will make the decision at that time, will decide the railway is not needed and will abandon it. I do not want to see a large number of these towns put in this situation of continuing uncertainty over the next 12 or 13 years.
Some of these towns are quite big places. For example, in the riding of the hon. member for Assiniboia, the shadow minister of transport, there are towns like Radville, with a population of 1,024, Bengough, with a population of 650; Willowbunch, with a population of 482; Gravelbourg, with a population of 1,428. All of these towns are recommended for
Hall Commission Report
inclusion under the prairie rail authority and will face a state of uncertainty for the next 12 years. I do not think there is going to be much development or progress in those towns unless the government decides to keep those rail lines and place them in the A category, maintaining them until the year 2000.
Other towns which will face continuing uncertainty are places like Cudworth, with a population of 800; Leroy, with a population of 435; Naicam, with a population of 711; and Wakaw, with a population of 1,009-all towns within the minister's riding. I think I am right in saying that the right hon. member for Prince Albert started his law practice in Wakaw a number of years ago, and I am sure he would not want that beautiful little town to face uncertainty until 1990 in regard to whether or not the rail line will be retained, new communities can be built and the farmers can be served by rail transportation.
When the minister speaks today, I would ask him to say something about the future of towns like Preeceville, in the riding of Mackenzie, with a population of 1,018 people, and the town of Kelvington, with a population of 1,053 people. These are large places, not tiny hamlets with 20 or 60 people. In many cases, over 1,000 people live in these towns and there are hundreds of farmers in the surrounding area. There are also several hamlets and villages between the towns, such as Preeceville, Kelvington and Porcupine in the Mackenzie constituency. Those areas are thriving and should not have to face continued uncertainty for several years. I hope the Minister of Transport is able to give them new hope when he rises and makes his statement later today.
The second recommendation contained in the Hall report is to retain the Crow rate. Our party has always been in favour the Crow rate. We think it is a rate which the farmers deserve. I hope the minister speaks categorically and strongly in favour of that rate. The commission also recommends that the difference between the Crowsnest rate and the cost of the railway be paid to the railways themselves and that the benefits of the Crow rate, to use the words of the Minister of Transport, not be given in some other way to the farmers. In fact, the Hall commission report, at page 337, reads as follows:
The very idea of sending out cheques to 160,000 farmers is appalling.
The Minister of Transport has talked about extra benefits to the farmers or to municipalities which resulted in that being contained in the report. The third thing they recommend is with respect to the whole area of economic development in western Canada. I would like to refer to the report once again where it is stated that freight structures for the processed product in its concentrated form should cost no more to transport on a ton-mile basis than the same product in its raw state. In other words, they are saying that in western Canada we should be able to process our goods and materials and ship them out at the same rate on a per ton-mile basis as raw materials. They are saying that the processing of the goods should be done where they are produced. For example, rape-
5974

May 26, 1977
Hall Commission Report
seed should be crushed and processed in the prairies where it is produced and should be subject to the same freight rate as the raw rapeseed. If the Minister of Transport wants to do something significant for the prairies and for western Canada, that is something that should be done.
The fourth item in the report deals with the retention of the decentralized system of country elevators. That is a system which the farmers have fought for over the years, and the Hall commission is saying that it be the basis of our grain handling system in the prairies. In effect, in their report they reject massive centralization of huge inland terminals, which some people in this country have been talking about for the last few years. As the hon. member for Prince Albert stated, the report refers to a northern railway rather than a pipeline in northern Canada. That is one suggestion which merits further study, because you can move many things on a railway that you cannot move in a pipeline, including many things people need, such as raw materials which may have to be shipped down some day from northern Canada.
The Hall report also deals with ports and improving the port facilities we have in this country by dredging the port at Thunder Bay and by improving the utilization of the port at Churchill so that it will be used to a much greater extent. The port at Churchill should be utilized to a greater extent, not only for the people of Churchill but for the people of the prairies generally. The report also recommends an inland cleaning facility in my home riding of Yorkton capable of handling and cleaning 25 million to 30 million bushels of grain every year. That is a suggestion which has a lot of merit and should be looked at seriously by the minister. They are also recommending a greater utilization of the port of Prince Rupert in British Columbia. There are a number of other recommendations one could talk about when debating an issue such as this. The report has more than 500 pages. It is an excellent report and one the government should be acting upon very quickly.
At this stage I would like to move an amendment to the motion which is before the House that will, hopefully, draw the government's attention to some of the more important parts of the Hall commission report. Therefore, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That the motion be amended by changing the period at the end thereof to a comma, and by adding immediately thereafter the following words:
"particularly (a) that the Crowsnest statutory rates be maintained, (b) that the principle of the Crowsnest rates be extended to agricultural products processed in western Canada, and (c) that the utilization of the ports of Churchill and Prince Rupert be increased".
I hope the Minister of Transport and his colleague, the Minister without Portfolio from Alberta, and other ministers in the cabinet will make some quick decisions on the Hall commission report which is before them. I hope they will end the uncertainty that literally hundreds of prairie towns and villages are now facing as to whether they will have rail facilities in the years ahead. Once and for all, those of us in western Canada will have our chance to share equally in the development of this great country of ours.
[Mr. Nystrom.J

Mr. Speaker, in beginning this afternoon I want to pay tribute to the members of the Hall commission who performed a great piece of work for the transportation system in Canada and for people who are engaged in producing and distributing grain. Mr. Cowan, Mr. Stewart, Mr. Forbes and Mr. Lehr from the prairie provinces travelled far and wide throughout the prairies and elsewhere in Canada in order to obtain the views, opinions and reactions of all people interested in the handling and transportation system. In carrying out their appointed task of examining the future of some 6,000 miles of branch lines in the prairie system and the over-all question of the handling and transporting of grain, I believe they did a superb job. They listened and attempted to come to grips with many of the problems which have vexed us for a long time.
I am pleased to see the words of the resolution as proposed by the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) and his statement of support in principle for the recommendations of the Hall commission. I was also pleased to hear the comments of the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom), in terms of his general support of the recommendations of the Hall commission. Perhaps it is somewhat better to put it in that form, since it is a little difficult to agree with some of the recommendations in principle. You have to either agree or disagree with it, rather than adopting it in principle and finding out later what it is all about, determining what it costs and whether you really like it. That is the phraseology this House sometimes uses, and I think we all understand it.
The Hall commission did not come out of the clear blue sky. It was a result of a great deal of work which had been done in connection with the grains industry. That work really began in 1969 with the appointment of the grains group and consolidation within the government of a special effort to come to grips with all the problems affecting our grains industry. What is astonishing in looking at the record of accomplishments since 1969 is to compare that in contrast with the practical absence of progress, change and alteration in the preceding period, and particularly the practical absence of changes and improvements in connection with the grains industry, whether handling, transportation, marketing or any of its policies, during the time when the right hon. member for Prince Albert was prime minister of this country.
There is one major exception to the record of very little being done, and that is the introduction during that period of the idea of cash advances on farm-stored grains. That was accomplished in the first months of that government, but then it seemed to run out of steam in coming to grips with any of the difficult problems. The reason why as a party it is unable to gain solid strength with people throughout this country is that it is so unwilling to take practical and sensible approaches and, indeed, to do anything for fear that someone might not like what it is doing. The Conservative party falls back on the traditional idea that if you do nothing, no one can attack you for your mistakes. That is the philosophy of that party, both in government and in opposition, and we have seen its record. We have seen this most recently, again, in relation to the problem
May 26, 1977

facing the beef industry. They criticize ideas to solve the problems, but they themselves have no ideas to put forward.

The work of the Hall commission was not the beginning of the study of the problem of grain handling and the transportation system. That began in 1969. One of the first tasks which we launched then, with the firm intention to be thorough, was the exhaustive study of all aspects of the problem. There was production of many documents which are available, of course, and were made available for a greater understanding of problems concerning elevators such as rail cost problems and their impact upon communities of having elevators or rail lines. All these studies which were accomplished over a period of several years were very important contributions from leaders within the grain industry as well as from many government officials who worked zealously on these. 1 wish to pay tribute, for instance, to the managers of two of the pools in the prairies, Mr. Mumford and Mr. Wally Madill, who, together with Mr. Searle who just then retired from another elevator company, worked with us in connection with many of these studies. At that time we began to assess the information to develop an understanding of the technical questions involved which were eventually to form the basis for the work of the Hall commission. When the work was over, it appeared to us that it was right to have two commissions to bring the work to a conclusion. We appointed then the Snavely commission to examine the technical questions of how much it really costs to move grain and to analyse these technical questions with the provinces and with the companies involved. Also, we appointed the Hall commission.
I was delighted when Mr. Hall accepted to be chairman of this commission, with his strong reputation for being able to listen to the public, to analyse problems and to present views in a sensitive and sympathetic manner. We appointed that commission to hear the public views, to bring together the knowledge, the analysis and the work that we and others had done, and to draw conclusions upon which to act. I was delighted to hear the reference of the right hon. member for Prince Albert to his original appointment of Mr. Hall to the bench in Canada. I think it is a well known and well recognized fact that in all of his work, whether on the bench or in the many commissions he has served so well, his strong liberalism has shown time and time again in his approach and in his conclusions in relation to problems.
That is why I believe it will be possible to act quickly on many of the Hall commission's recommendations and to use them as the basis for the development of solutions to problems in the grain industry. Indeed, to pick up the challenge of the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville, I can say that as soon as I saw the recommendations in the Hall commission report I began work on the initial question dealing with his first and principal recommendation that a particular 1,813 miles of track which were part of his study should be transferred to the basic rail network. I put that proposition to my colleagues for
Hall Commission Report
consideration, and this morning the order in council was passed to transfer those 1,813 miles recommended by Mr. Hall to the basic rail network. They will be protected from abandonment in the year 2000, which applies to the other branch lines which were first put into that basic network system. We have, therefore, already on the tenth day after the publication of the Hall report implemented its major feature.
Also, today by order in council we extended protection to 2,344 miles of line which the Hall commission recommended be put in the hands of the prairie rail authority. We have extended their protection to January 1, 1979, so that we may take immediate steps and, at the same time, deliberate action in relation to this recommendation to consider all its implications and to see what formal action must be taken before parliament can carry out that recommendation.
1 noted the cautionary words of the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville, expressed previously by some of the representatives of farmers in the prairies, with regard to some aspects that raise concern. I propose to begin immediately discussions with representatives of farmers and, of course, to hear the farmers themselves on the problems, the merits and the difficulties of this recommendation. This with the view to saying, as I said earlier in the House, that I like the report in general and in principle. I hope we can find a way to solve the dilemmas which are seen to exist in it and to get on with it in accordance with the spirit of the Hall commission report.
I propose to meet tomorrow in Regina with the leaders of many of the farm organizations and representatives of the elevator companies, or at least the key ones, and representatives of others involved in the grain industry, including the Wheat Board, we hope, in order to move forward on this and other recommendations in the Hall report. It will not be possible to say of this government, in relation to this problem concerning the grain industry, that we have been slow in moving. We will continue to do here, in relation to this great industry, what our record shows we have done since 1969, that is, to tackled the problems one by one and many together in order to make progress and in order to put the prairie farmer, who is the producer of our Canadian grain both for domestic and export use, into a sound position in his operations, in his marketing and in his income. speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I presume you are making due allowance for the extension of my time because of these interjections.
I refer to the formation of the Canadian Grains Council and also to the expanded credit facilities and long-term federal guarantees which allowed the Wheat Board to pursue new markets for grain. I refer to the new and vigorous efforts to break into world barley markets where we had really never been in a big way for many years before 1970. Again, if we look at the record, while the government of the right hon. member for Prince Albert was in power we find there was little and seriously dwindling attention paid to the feed barley market of the world. After 1970 we determined that we should

be in that market in a big way. We set initial prices which encouraged the growth of barley so it would be available for export. We set targets of 200 million bushels fo exports as a basic target the Wheat Board should go after, and in some of the years since then when it has been produced and available that amount of grain has indeed been sold. That is why in the past several years we have had record sales which have exceeded any of the levels which were achieved at any time before 1965.
We set in place a program which put $10 million annually into a new market development fund. We have developed new research facilities such as the new crop science division at the University of Saskatchewan and the protein, oil and starch plant which will be opened in July at that university. We introduced the two-price wheat program, which in a permanent way had never before been seen although it had been talked about by prairie people for many years. We did that at a time when it cost many million dollars each year to finance. We brought in a new quota system, which hon. members opposite attacked but which now allows the smooth and easy flow of grain into the system instead of bringing grain into the system willy-nilly and helter-skelter without regard to market needs and to what the transportation system can handle. We introduced a system for the early announcement of quotas, guaranteed deliveries and initial prices before seeding so that farmers would have that additional information. We improved the timing of final payments by the Wheat Board. We introduced the deferred cash ticket system on grain deliveries.
We introduced a separate pool for malting barley. The block shipping system helped tremendously in the grain handling and transportation system with which Mr. Hall and his commission had to deal. We helped with the grain trucking program, which provided some valuable information to the commission. We introduced government financing for the bringing in of grain so it could be dried. We introduced such things as further consultations with producers, and the election of the advisory committee to the Canadian Wheat Board. We held a poll among rapeseed producers to determine their marketing preference. We now have before the House a proposal for a voluntary system of pooling rapeseed.
Over these past years, while we knew that further study on the grain handling and transportation system was needed and that the Hall report was needed, we decided that there were some things we could do in advance of the report. Such things that everyone seemed to agree would be consistent with any possible combination of grain delivery systems they could imagine. The hopper car program is a prime example of that. In addition we introduced the boxcar repair program to keep extra cars in operation for grain. We have now completed the construction or ordering of 8,000 hopper cars for grain at a cost of $240 million to $250 million.
Hon. members opposite who are from the west ignore and do not mention the things we have done for this important western industry, while their colleagues from other parts of the country point to these iniatives with criticism, saying that the government shows a preference for the west. 1 ask hon. mem-
May 26, 1977

bers opposite to try to bring about unity amongst themselves so that their party can be a party for unity for this country as well.

The hon. member should recognize that at this point in time we are already ahead of last year's exports, and by the time this crop year is over, this particular crop year we will have exported very much more grain than we did last year. The only reason there will be additional grain on the farms- which there will be-is the record production which we all should welcome and the build-up of supplies which were already at that point fairly high. It is a welcome build-up of supplies in terms of security of supply for the world.
Hon. members opposite asked me to refer to the Crowsnest rates on grain, and I am certainly glad to take this opportunity to do that. The Conservative party, through its spokesman, the right hon. member for Prince Albert, and the New Democratic
Hal! Commission Report
Party, through its spokesman, the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville, have both said that essentially they agree with the recommendations of the Hall report. As with the Berger report, they were ready to agree unanimously to those recommendations the very day the report came out and before they had much chance to read it. Notwithstanding the fact that the official opposition should have been somewhat alerted to the dangers of that-because the Leader of the Opposition immediately supported the Berger report in total and then had to vote the other way in this House-on reflection perhaps a little bit of weighing of the evidence is desirable. I have also said that about some of the individual recommendations, but it would be useful to know what they cost. Even if one is willing to pay the cost, it is useful to know what it is before one decides to proceed.
Hon. members opposite support the recommendations of the Hall report in general.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GRAIN HANDLING AND TRANSPORTATION
speechtext: Have you not supported them in general? Make up your mind.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GRAIN HANDLING AND TRANSPORTATION
speechtext:
On the question of the Crowsnest rate, the Hall commission says this:
Regardless of what rate may be set for the transport of grain to export position that rate must be statutory, not variable.
I have no hesitation in saying that I have never had any thoughts to the contrary in relation to that particular rate on grain. The commission report goes on:
How the difference between the new rate and the Crowsnest rate will be apportioned between the government and the producer is, of course, a matter for government decision. This commission feels that the government must continue to subsidize the transportation of export grain and that the full cost, as deemed by the commission on the costs of transporting grain by rail, must not be imposed on the producer.
In supporting that recommendation in general, as the two parties opposite have done, it should be noted they did not go as far as I have gone in the past in my assertion that I believed the whole of the benefit of the Crowsnest rate for grain should be reserved for western producers. They do not go as far as I have gone in suggesting that. Indeed, over the years my only qualification about the preservation of the whole of the benefit of the Crowsnest rate for the west has been to tie it in principle and theory, as it was tied in national policy almost a century ago, to the existence and creation of tariffs and their burdens on the grain farmer and the agricultural sector. I have suggested that any diminution in the benefit of those rates to the prairies could only come about if benefit was being conferred on the prairies and on the grain sector in particular by improvements and movements toward freer trade.
If the world were to move toward freer trade, then I could see that the particular historic benefit which was tied in many ways to the development of a tariff structure should be varied as well. That is the only comment or qualification I have made, whereas here the commission suggests perhaps there should be greater movement away from the statutory rate. I say that the statutory rate should remain in that statutory

May 26, 1977
Hall Commission Report
form. I will be having discussions with my colleagues about many other issues in the Hall report in connection with improvements in the grain handling and transportation system.
Surely, in our total examination of freight we have to bring some sense of the principles to bear in regard to the handling of products and the impact of one product upon another. The Hall commission seems to me clearly to support the statement that we ought to have equity in freight rates between grain and meat. That is something I have said emphatically over and over again, particularly in connection with the development of the feed grains policy for Canada. I have spoken of the need to have access to feed grain for all farmers in all parts of the country for the purpose of freedom of trade and proper development of products according to natural advantage. I have spoken, as well, of the need to have equity in freight rates between the two products. In many ways, in principle, the people throughout the prairies appreciate the importance of that and realize it is a problem that has to be grappled with. The recommendation to upgrade the railways will cost a great deal of money. That is also a matter that this government will have to grapple with in the near future.
I spoke about the record of this government in relation to many other grain programs, without mentioning them all. I did not mention what is perhaps the greatest of all government programs in the past eight or nine years, the western grains stabilization plan. This may well prove over the years to be the greatest bulwark and mainstay of prairie grain producers at any time where downswings occur. In the light of history, there are reasons to believe that those downswings will occur. This great grain stabilization plan commits the government, in essence, to 4 per cent annually of the value of grain but guarantees whatever amount is required from the treasury to pay the difference between what the cash income of prairie farmers has been over five years and what it is in a current year. That may well prove to be the greatest monument to the action of this government in regard to the grain industry.
Mr. Speaker, that plan was the result of years and years of hard and determined work on the part of the few of us on this side of the House from the prairies, with the co-operation of members of the Liberal party from every province in the country-from Quebec and Ontario, from the Atlantic provinces and British Columbia as well as the Liberals from the prairies. It triumphed over the struggle and time-wasting and time-consuming efforts of members opposite from the prairies who were doing a disservice by working against a plan because of only one thing-that they did not want a plan so good to be brought in. That kind of narrow politics I cannot understand, even from members opposite.
The government has a record of performance in relation to the grain industry which is recognized by members of that industry, farmers and farm leaders alike. They know the problems and know that we have taken action with programs like the change in the quota system which in its time was unpopular but which has proved to be what was needed. People across this country who have seen that know they can have confidence. So much of what is in the Hall commission report
[Mr. Lang.)
is the culmination of the work done in the grains group and the culmination of the hearings we asked the Hall commission to undertake. Those people know that we will take very serious steps to implement those recommendations which will benefit the prairies, the grain industry and the grain farmer.
It will be said after these eight, nine or ten years of performance that this government has acted forthrightly at all times-has acted quickly and decisively for the benefit of the grain industry and its systems. We will do so again in connection with the Hall report. That is my pledge, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to make a few comments on today's motion, although I am somewhat surprised to see how quickly we are deciding on the Hall report. I am sure it is not a mistake to say that most of us did not have time to read it because we just got it; yet we are simply requested to agree in principle on the recommendation of the Hall commission.
I think it is only an agreement in principle because it is impossible to study such a voluminous document in two, three or four days. After reading the first few pages of this document, we realize that it concerns primarily the interest of the western provinces, the grain production, as the minister just said. It concerns all the provinces of Canada because I think that the evolution of a province has an impact on the whole country; it concerns us all the more, as the minister also said, that the change will not be made with nothing but with money; we are then much more interested because we will also be asked to pay for this change.
Therefore I congratulate all the members of the Hall commission. The minister said that this commission had travelled a lot. I would add they have written a lot as well, because judging from their first volume of almost 600 pages we have just received, let alone those to come, I believe we can say these commissioners have done a lot of work. I am very pleased for western farmers who must also benefit from the effects of the progress taking place in this country.
If we go back to the time when the grain transportation system through the Prairies was just beginning, we find that what was modern then is entirely obsolete today, like the agricultural production which is quite different, much more mechanized and more rapid than at the time when they farmed with horses. This is why we can still see all these things from the past, that is those hundreds of local elevators, many of which are now completely abandoned. The same applies to railway tracks. The Hall commission was supposed to undertake a study of the situation in order to make constructive recommendations to Parliament. Appointed in 1975, this commission was assigned the task of studying the needs of western farmers in terms of railway transportation, to make a full assessment of requirements relating to regional transportation
May 26, 1977

in order to analyze the impact of the over-all grain handling and transportation system.
Finally, it was to make recommendations which today affect about 6,283 miles of railway tracks throughout the Prairie provinces. As regards those lines which are to be abandoned, I believe many western producers will have a lot to say, and we shall not voice any objection about it because they have common interests to defend. It is quite similar to what is happening in our province where we fight in an attempt to modernize our railway system. We share almost the same problems, passenger services, freight services, and we must at all cost deal with transportation experts. We must take their advice, but especially study their recommendations. I suggest this is what the Prairie farmers are trying to do with this motion today.
We shall deal also with the maintenance of statutory rates and handling but I wish we would refer to storage as well.
In a summary of his first volume, this is what Mr. Justice Hall had to say:
The grain handling and transportation commission asserts that this report is the result of a two-year study. During those two years, about 120 hearings have been held and the commission has received over 1,600 briefs. In addition, more than 15,000 people have attended the commission hearings.
Mr. Speaker, I insist on quoting that paragraph. People often say: They set up that commission, but now we will hear no more about it. I shall quote that excerpt to show the people that those commissions do work efficiently, for I think that if the people were aware of the number of hours of work, of miles covered, of visits out in the field, they would appreciate the work of this commission far more:
During its inquiry, the commission encouraged all those who are interested in the future of western Canada to express their views, both orally and in writing, at its hearings. Most of them were held in the towns and cities along the railway lines the commission was to assess and about which it was to make recommendations.
So, the commissioners did not work haphazardly; they did not write that volume sitting in their offices: they went out into the field, to see first hand what is going on.
The recommendations of the commission should serve as the basis for rationalizing the grain handling and transportation system in the future. In addition to recommending the early abandonment of the lines which are no longer needed, we also recommend the creation of a new body whose function would be to make a permanent assessment of future needs in the field of railway transportation. The commission concludes that 1,813 miles of branch lines in the Prairies, which have proved very useful and important on a regional basis, should be reintegrated into the main railway network, and that their existence be guaranteed until the year 2000.
The commission therefore recommends the abandonment, pure and simple, of over 2,000 miles of branch lines which have not been used for some time. I know that some years ago I had occasion to visit the Prairie provinces two or three times, and I was amazed to see all those abandoned lines. At the same time, there exists a whole new system, more modern and much quicker, of getting to the elevators. As I said a while ago, the years of the small industry, the small farm in the west are over, and the means of transport must, of necessity, be adapted to the evolution of agricultural production. We always hear that the west is Canada's granary, and I think this is true
Ajournment Motion
as far as grains are concerned. It is absolutely necessary to have this wealth shipped as soon as possible instead of leaving it in the fields. It is also necessary that all the provinces benefit from this. Those who are called upon to pay must also benefit from the future modernization in the western provinces.
This leads me to the question of storage. It is all well to take the grain from the land of the Prairie provinces and bring it to the elevators, but it must also be redistributed in the other provinces. I draw particularly the minister's attention to this point, namely that we will have to rethink the matter of grain storage in each and every province, and in Quebec-I speak for Quebec because that is where I live-it will be necessary to double the number of elevators either in Quebec City or in Montreal so that we do not have to send the grain by train in winter, when it is 50 per cent cheaper by ship.
If we had the necessary storage for a 12-month period, consumers, farmers and producers would benefit from the savings instead of being forced as they are now to fill western elevators and even municipal elevators right up. It would be so easy, before the close of the shipping season, to forward to Quebec and Maritime elevators the necessary stocks to guarantee to the consumers of each of those provinces the grain they will need during the 12 following months.
I think the government must show leadership and anticipate and we should forecast for at least 12 months to avoid those transport shortages. There are not enough engines and cars to carry the grain in eastern Canada when it would have been so easy to try before the close of the shipping season to fill up the elevators and thus the surplus alone would have to be carried in case of emergency during winter. Those are the comments which I want to make for now. I am pleased once again with the work done by the commission and I am convinced that it will benefit Canada as a whole.
