speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) had stayed to hear what I am going to say, because I would rather say these things face to face. This motion was moved today to force the government to declare where it stands on the principles of the Hall report. There is nothing new in the principles enunciated in this report. They have been talked about and proposed in western Canada over the past 50 years. The essence of this report is that it puts all these things that we have asked for for half a century into one volume. Second, it puts it into plain English that even a government can understand.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GRAIN HANDLING AND TRANSPORTATION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GRAIN HANDLING AND TRANSPORTATION
speechtext:
What does the minister do in the face of this challenge by the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker)? He brought in a long list of achievements of his government and attacked the record of the Diefenbaker administration 15 years ago. Why does he take this stance? The reason he avoids the challenge of the right hon. member for Prince Albert is that he knows the record of his government. The philosophy of his government is not the philosophy of western Canada. If the minister has done so much good, why is he so feared all through the west?
In Saskatchewan we are in the process of fighting provincial by-elections. A party which had nothing two years ago, relatively 15 or 20 per cent of the vote, is now winning these by-elections. It is not so much because of dissatisfaction with the government in Saskatchewan, but with the fact that the issues are being fought on federal issues. The person who, above all, the farmers want to send a message to when they vote in these provincial by-elections in Saskatchewan is the Minister of Transport. They want him to know their philosophy is one of expansion in the west. Their philosophy is one of using the great productivity that they have to help feed the whole world. All they get from this government is restriction, restriction, restriction. They know that this man has to be removed from the decision-making of the government of Canada. We know what he is doing.
When the minister brought in the LIFT program in 1970 it was not an isolated act by a government. It was part of a philosophy that came out of an agricultural task force report in 1969. It said that all across Canada there were three times as many farmers as there should be, and we should deliberate-
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Ethier).]
ly, with government policies at the federal level and the provincial level, cut that number down to one-

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GRAIN HANDLING AND TRANSPORTATION
speechtext: That is not what it said, and you know it.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GRAIN HANDLING AND TRANSPORTATION
speechtext:
That policy of the agricultural task force said that as far as the prairies are concerned, we should reduce the acreage to half. The next year the minister and his government brought in four bits of legislation to help carry out that principle. The LIFT program was number one. Look carefully at the LIFT program recommended by the farm organizations and accepted by the government because the men who wrote the agricultural task force report tried to tell the farmers that they had too much wheat productivity and that they should cut out wheat. They had a program called the small farm program to get rid of farmers. They set up a land bank. I was in Saskatchewan in Pelly constituency the last two days, and 20 per cent of the land is owned by the government. It is all part of a policy to take over the control of the individual and the decision-making on the farms of this country.
The Minister of Transport brought out the key question of the Crowsnest rate. He said he was for the Crowsnest rates and for putting them into a statute. Who is not? They have to be there. However, what he does not seem to face up to is the significance of what Hall has said about these Crowsnest rates and what the minister and his government intended. The minister wanted to change the Crowsnest rates from what they are, charge the farmers two or three times more and then come back and reimburse the farmer for the extra cost. He wanted to pay it back to the farmer as an individual farmer, either in acreage or by bushels. Hall saw the danger. Hall is from the west. He knew the deep fear in the hearts of western farmers when he wrote this, and I quote:
The commission recommends that the difference between the Crowsnest rate and the rate determined through costs found by the commission on the costs of transporting grain should be paid directly to the railways, and not to individual farmers. The very idea of sending out cheques to 160,000 farmers is appalling.
It is not appalling to the Minister of Transport. He knows that is how you can control the votes. He, the great Santa Claus of all times, wants to send out 160,000 cheques to individual farmers. We remember under the LIFT program before the election in 1972 the cheques that came out for the summer fallow, land which should have been in wheat. After the 1972 election they said, "You were overpaid, and we have to get it back." Before the 1974 election they came along and made payments for grassing.

Yes, Mr. Speaker, at the end of my speech. Then they came along and said they had overpaid them, and they had to get it back. All this was done so overtly that members of this House, the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers) and the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. Hamilton), were able to report to the Auditor General that things were going on that
May 26, 1977

did not seem right. The Auditor General went in and photographed the documents of the organization carrying out that program.
We turned our information over to the criminal fraud squad of the RCMP. It is pretty hard to get guys who are into the pot to give evidence against themselves, but five did. One was charged, the head man. When the evidence was put before the judge, he said there was enough evidence to have this man stand trial for criminal fraud. In plain terms, that meant stealing money from the farmers and trying to persuade them to vote Liberal. That case has never been heard. Why? That will be the issue one of these days. We questioned the Minister of Agriculture on the same subject because beside the criminal fraud there was the political fraud. The minister stood in the House and said, "Well, they burned the records". When a matter is before parliament affecting the repeal of the PFAA, and when a matter of criminal fraud is before the courts, a government which would allow these guilty people to go in and burn the records of PFAA has a purpose in mind beyond just burning the records. The Minister of Transport has one purpose in mind-

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GRAIN HANDLING AND TRANSPORTATION
speechtext: On a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member seems to be implying that I had some connection with the acts he was describing. He has heard that that is not true. He should withdraw any such suggestion or imputation. He has gone further than that and referred to "those guilty persons"-I believe those were his words-in relation to people who are not here to defend themselves and who are thus imputed by him to be guilty before court process has been completed. I think he ought to refrain from that kind of conduct even though he is protected in this House by longstanding privileges accorded to members of parliament. These are privileges which ought not to be abused and the hon. member ought, therefore, to avoid making statements of the kind he did. I say this without having connection with the individuals concerned, but out of a regard for a sense of fairness. I come back to my original remarks, that if he was imputing any connection between myself and any wrongdoing, 1 ask him to withdraw.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GRAIN HANDLING AND TRANSPORTATION
speechtext:
What I am going to say, Mr. Speaker, is going to be loud and clear. The man who is charged with criminal fraud by stealing money from the farmers was an appointee of the government opposite, of which the minister is part. The hon. gentleman can make what he likes of that. Second, it was a colleague of his, the Minister of Agriculture, who stood up in this House, as the record shows, and said the documents were burned. When this subject goes before a committee, as one day it will, we shall ask the government why those women were dismissed just before Christmas. Why did they keep a director there who was fully paid but never allowed to go into his own office? There is no question of privilege there. The minister knows exactly what 1 am saying, and exactly who is responsible for putting
Hall Commission Report
that man, who is now before the courts on charges of criminal fraud, in his position.
Now I want to return to my speech. The minister has tried to obscure the fact that the Hall report strikes a body blow at him and all he has tried to do in western Canada in the last eight years. It is obvious that members on the government side do not like this message. But it is a message they have got to hear. People in this country do not want corrupt government, whether they live in Quebec or in Saskatchewan. They want vrai gouvernement, good government, true government, honest government.
Let us take another issue. In Bill C-33 the government brought in a measure to amend the Transportation Act. All the work parliament did from 1964 to 1967 in transferring the power to control railways, pipelines, airlines, trucking, everything involved in transportation, out of the hands of the minister and the civil servants-who were doing nothing with it, anyway-and into the hands of a board of 17 members of the transport commission-a board which did nothing with it, either-was brought to nothing. At this very moment there stands upon our agenda a bill to take all that power away from the commission which, as 1 say, did nothing with it, and put it again into the hands of the minister and the civil servants around him. When we see a political machine being built up in western Canada, sure we are going to fight. We had that under Gardiner for 25 years, and we are not going to tolerate that type of dictatorship any more from people who are expressing philosophies which are foreign to our western views and, I think, foreign to those of the whole country.
In conclusion, I want to say a word about the amendment put forward by the NDP. I do not think there is any question but that it is acceptable. But why did they limit their amendment to two specific principles-the Crowsnest rates and the utilization of Churchill and Port Rupert? What about the most important principle in the whole report, the rationalization of the grain handling system? There is no mention of the fact that we have five great inland terminals out there, owned by the people of Canada, standing empty and unused. Why? Because to use them would be to provide competition with existing grain companies. Why did the NDP not put that into their program? Why don't they talk about the rationalization of the grain handling industry? No longer will they be allowed to,build where they shouldn't, and to abandon where they should not. They will come under the control of the prairie railway authority, if the Hall recommendations are accepted. They will come under the control of the Board of Grain Commissioners and of the Canadian Wheat Board.
One of the great failures of the last 15 years has been the unwillingness of the grain companies in western Canada to modernize. The minister says the Diefenbaker government did nothing. The only person who will believe that statement is his wife. In 1962 I went to a meeting in Regina and in a public speech, speaking as a minister of the Crown, I asked the delegates of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool to support me in two proposals. One was that they set aside 2 cents a bushel on every bushel they put into their elevators to help their own

May 26, 1977
Hall Commission Report
companies modernize their elevator systems and get rid of the inefficient, costly and wasteful system they had. The second thing I asked them was to join with their rivals, the UGG, and go into operation with the Alberta and Manitoba pools and form a selling agency to sell Canadian wheat abroad, instead of just sitting there collecting money out of storage and handling.
The price I paid for making those two proposals was this: the leader of the official opposition at that time, Mr. Pearson, attacked me in the House, supported by the leader of the NDP, the present member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas). The position they took was that one should not ask farm organizations to do anything for themselves. To do so is Conservative philosophy; their philosophy is to allow nothing to be done and continue to allow farmers to face those heavy costs. Yet after five days of debate in that farm meeting in Saskatchewan, those farmers voted 100 per cent in favour of my proposals. The question then arises: Why was nothing done? Their delegates supported it, but nothing developed. Only in the last five or six years have the grain companies begun to modernize under the threat of other companies coming in and building big elevators. Why is that not mentioned? Cannot the minister stand in the House and say, "I support the rationalization of the grain handling system"?
Then there is this business of not allowing farmers to haul their grain to CPR railway lines, barring them from sending their grain to Churchill or to Prince Rupert. All our northern grain at CPR points had to be hauled hundreds of miles south to the east or the west to avoid CP cars travelling over CNR lines. What a crime against the farmers of western Canada! Hall recommends that this be stopped. There is no mention of that in the amendment. The minister could have said, "I will accept that immediately". He does not need a statutory change; he passes an order in council that lines already abandoned can be abandoned. Then he puts in another order in council today, when he knew that this motion was coming up, which says, in effect, that the 2,000 lines which are considered marginal and will be put under the prairie railway authority will not be decided upon until January 1, 1979. That only tells me one thing, that we would not-

speechtext:
I will not take too long, Mr. Speaker. I want to conclude with a rapid summary. It is the minister who is under attack here. He has failed to respond today to the challenge of the Crow rates. This report is not to be used for political monkey-shining; it is to be used to put the railways into a rational and profit-making position. In this debate today the minister has failed to support
[Mr. Hamilton (Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain).)
the principle of the rationalization of the railways-getting rid of lines running parallel, of cases where grain is hauled 100 miles to the east and 100 miles to the west, so that the railways not run over each other's lines.
The minister should have supported rationalization because it would mean less cost to the taxpayer and more money to the railways. There has been no response from the minister in regard to giving the prairie rail authority power to direct, which is key to the success of the Hall proposals. The minister has failed to mention the inland terminals' 50 years of crime against the farmers. This is now a clear recommendation in the Hall report. They belonged to us as a government.
Let me give the House one example. When you ship grain to the coast from these big new terminals at Thunder Bay or Vancouver there is a certain kind of tonnage which we call screenings. When you ship, say, to Vancouver the farmer pays the cost of shipping the screenings. Then it costs the grain company money to pelletize and sell the screenings. There are about 28 million bushels of screenings a year, and in marketable form they cost about $16 a ton. The price of the screenings, when sold to the poultry producer on the west coast, is $80 a ton. In other words, $64 profit goes to the grain companies, value that belongs to the farmer. By running the inland terminals, what you are saying to the farmer is that the screenings should be taken out in the west and utilized in the beef industry, with the value going to the people who produce the grain.
The minister has failed to see the significance of the Hall report and what it means to the development of Churchill and Prince Rupert, not to hinder and hurt but to help the ports of Vancouver, Montreal and those in the Atlantic region. The minister has failed to see that the whole thrust of the Hall report is not to add great extra subsidy costs but to run the railroads and the grain system rationally, so that costs are cut and the railways begin to make money.
This is why a northern railway was added, Mr. Speaker. The minister said that the northern railway was beyond the commission's terms of reference, but Mr. Justice Hall shot that down; he read the actual terms of reference. The minister does not even realize what Hall is talking about. He is talking about hauling more commodities by rail, such as gravel, mineral concentrates from the north, finished beef products, processed rapeseed, and so on. The cries of the west for the last 50 years have been answered by this report, yet the minister turns, twists and deviates, all to avoid saying it is a great report and that the government can accept every single principle which will be implemented as fast as humanly possible.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, if these principles are not in the statute books of this country and enshrined in some form of regulation when the government call the election, then they had better watch out. We have spent 40 years now waiting for some action. The government scuttled away from taking action on the MacPherson report. Are they going to scuttle away again? This is the issue in the west. If action is not taken, then hon. members opposite will have no further chance to say "No" all the time.
May 26, 1977

Incidentally, I heard the interjection of the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Goodale) today. 1 was in the House watching the hon. member for Assiniboia when the motion of the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar was moved. I saw the hon. member for Assiniboia say "No". I simply say to members from Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Alberta and B.C., "Vote for these principles. The people are not going to stand for any more delay. They want action. This report will not cost the taxpayer any more money. It will reduce subsidies. It is a good report".
I could make five suggestions which would improve the report, but they are all additions of principle. However, that is not my purpose here today. We have asked this parliament to accept the principles contained in the Hall report and to do those things that he recommends before we go to the country. Then we will know the government really means what they say. We do not want any more orders in council to the effect that the government is going to consider the matter on January 1, 1979. The government does not need any more information. We have had more reports on the subject over the last ten years than we need. I tell the government to act now so that hon. members opposite can stand up before westerners and tell them they were not betrayed when the chance came.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is always a real pleasure to listen to and become involved in debate with my hon. friend from Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton). Let me assure him that the government will undoubtedly follow his suggestion in terms of moving forward with the report of the Hall commission. In listening to my hon. friend I always have the feeling, when he recites the tremendous aims and goals that he and his party have for Canada, particularly western Canada, that he is suffering from deep frustration which goes back to the time when he and his party did have the opportunity to put forward blueprints for agriculture, for transportation and other vital areas, not only in Canada in general but in western Canada in particular. I can only conclude that this frustration stems from his difficulty in coming to grips with the problems, and particularly with the solutions, to those problems.
I want to thank the right hon. member and others opposite for the opportunity to debate this matter today and for putting the subject of the Hall commission report on the order paper. I think that a little bit of history might be in order in so far as the Hall commission report is concerned. In the early pages of the report it is pointed out that there have been 12 similar commissions or studies on this entire field over the last 60 to 70 years. I am sure that the essence of this report will not take as long to implement as the MacPhefson report and the legislation which followed. I think there was a time-frame of nine years from the time that commission was established in 1959 until we saw legislation in 1966, 1967 and 1968, some of which has not yet been proclaimed.
Now, less than 20 years later, we are again looking-as well we should as a parliament-at transportation needs and particularly at the grain handling system in western Canada. Only two years have gone by since the establishment of the Hall
Hall Commission Report
commission. It was established by a Liberal government through the auspices of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) in charge of the Wheat Board and his predecessor, the former member for Langelier when he was minister of transport. Therefore, two years have elapsed already since the commission was established. I know we are not going to have to wait another seven years, as was the record with the previous Conservative government commission.
The Conservatives' record in transportation is almost an enviable one because it is almost totally clean. The one accomplishment they had was to establish and appoint that Mac-Pherson Commission. In their period of government, they never got around to doing very much about transportation, other than that one single step. Thus it is pretty difficult to go back and criticize that record, because it is so clean in that regard. They have done nothing; they have suggested nothing; they have proposed nothing; and, generally speaking, they have turned a blind eye to the economic facts of life in the country, as time has gone on and changed those economic facts.
The Minister of Transport pointed out in his remarks that they want greater subsidies in the east and greater subsidies in the west, and all the while they want reduced government expenditures-it is not supposed to cost any money. They do not want user-pay, and they do not want the user to know what is going on and what the economic facts of life are. It is not going to be difficult for the government and for the Minister of Transport to surpass the record of the opposition in transportation. It has already been done a number of times over.
The hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) made reference to the history and the story behind the Hall Commission-where did it come from, why was it set up, and for what purposes did they go out and hold the tremendous series of hearings that they did across the prairie region? I would like to point out that it was two Liberal ministers and this government that established that commission, which did a fine job and gave us the finest report we have ever seen in transportation in the grain handling field. The report not only combines those aspects of it, but it also combines other social and economic aspects of western life. I am sure this report will be a blueprint for government action in that respect.
There was reference made to a number of the recommendations contained in the report. Some of the statements made and the recommendations deserve review and inclusion in the record to some extent. It is difficult to cover all of the things alluded to in this very comprehensive report. The commission members were to inquire into the rail needs of communities, and were to receive evidence from any person, interested agency, group or corporation. That was their mandate, and in that respect Chief Justice Hall and his fellow commissioners certainly carried out their mandate to the fullest. They had something like 15,000 people present at a wide variety of hearings, not only in the prairies but on the west coast as well. They did an excellent job in seeking opinions from western

May 26, 1977
Hall Commission Report
people concerned with every phase of the industry, from communities, from grain companies and so on.
Specifically they were to deal with the question of 6,283 miles of branch lines which had been proposed for abandonment. This followed designation by the Minister of Transport in December 1974 of 12,000 miles of rail network in western Canada as a so-called basic network. The idea was to set those lines out as being a permanent network regarding which there was no need for people, communities or grain companies to be concerned about their futures. The commission was established to look into the rail needs of communities on that 6,000 miles which was proposed for abandonment. It became operational; it did a very thorough job; it heard many, many people; and it heard many suggestions-indeed suggestions which have been made frequently in the past. Now we have them all compiled and built into the Hall Commission report.
It is a blueprint of the concerns and aspirations of western people, not only in the field of grain transportation but in other aspects as well. What did the Hall report say? It covered a wide variety of recommendations. Before looking to any great extent at what the Hall Commission said and what it recommended, we should briefly look at the conclusions of the previous royal commission, namely, the MacPherson Royal Commission.
The deterioration of the railroads took place as a result of the deficits which were the plague of the railroads. The MacPherson Commission concluded that railway deficits were due to three factors: the collective burdens of uneconomic branch lines, the unprofitable passenger services, and the insufficiency of the Crowsnest pass grain rates. Those factors prevented them from upgrading the system and updating the system.
I would like to look at some of the points made by the Hall Commission, as they conducted their work and wrote their report. When you look at the branch lines and the railway network in western Canada, you are not only looking at the railroads and grain movement, but you are also looking at the effect the abandonment of these lines will have, might have, or could have on the life of various communities concerned.
I would like to quote from page 79 of the Hall Commission report which reads as follows:
It is the people and the spirit of the people which gives the community viability, not the railways nor the elevators.
The commission does not doubt the psychological effect that the removal of the railway will have on many residents. Many of the inhabitants of affected communities will have already experienced the loss of such things as the livery barn, the steam train, the school, or the telephone exchange. Whether we deem the phasing out of these elements of community life to be signs of progress or not, it is a fact that these facilities were the victims of our developing technology and social change, unrelated to rail abandonment.
I believe that is a true statement and a rather strong statement. There are communities, however, which will be affected by abandonment and might not believe that statement. It has been one of the things which has caused a great deal of concern in western Canada to people in all walks of life, and not only farmers, when we discuss, debate or look at this whole question of rail rationalization-whether to aban-

don or not to abandon; on what terms to abandon; and so on. It was one of the questions which was difficult to resolve with respect to the 1967 act, when criteria were set out by which the CTC would judge whether or not to abandon a railway line. I am referring to the whole question of social and economic cost-how do you define it and how do you put a handle on it? The Hall Commission report stated that, as a group of people out there, we over-emphasized that particular aspect of this whole question of abandonment.
There are other aspects and quotes in the report which should be discussed. I notice the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain referred to the question of screenings- where those screenings are, what could happen to them, and where they should be. The report covers that particular subject. That has a relationship not only to the grain industry and the transportation industry, but also to the livestock industry. Referring to the cleaning of grain and screenings, the Hall Commission report at page 153 reads as follows:
Considerable discussion ensued at some hearings regarding the cleaning of grain and the use of screenings.
The report continues as follows:
On the average one out of every 40 cars of grain shipped is screenings. Whether this represents a loss of cheap feed to the prairie livestock producer or a windfall to the grain companies is open to question.
The report goes on to say at page 155:
Screenings represent a large quantity of product, the 28 million bushels produced is equivalent to the total record Churchill throughput of 1976.
I think that is a pretty interesting observation. It goes on to read:
These are hauled from the prairies at a cost to the transportation system and represent no return to the producer except as an unknown reduction in handling tariffs and as patronage dividends.
Again, with reference to the point made by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain, the report states:
The interior government terminal elevators at Moose Jaw, Saskatoon, Edmonton, Lethbridge and Calgary have a combined cleaning capacity of 205 million bushels per year. These facilities are in place and it is a waste of existing resources if they are not fully utilized.
As I said, this report makes a number of observations in a great variety of areas that have been discussed before, and it is to be hoped that steps can be taken not only to recognize these facts but to try to do something about them.
A little later the report goes on to discuss further the aspects of the screenings. At page 158 and 159 it states the following:
6.	All of the screenings produced in western Canada could be utilized in western Canada for livestock feed.
7.	The screenings will be used for feed on the prairies when available and economics dictate.
8.	In light of the alternatives presented, the cleaning of grain at inland facilities equipped to do so appears to offer the greatest flexibility of exploiting market opportunities.
Western grain and livestock producers are in an improved position and will realize maximum returns if grain cleaning is carried out at a location with free access to all markets.
Screenings now constitute a hidden tariff as far as the grain producer is concerned. This should not be so.
May 26, 1977

Equity between the handling of products from both the grain and the livestock industries has been a sore point with me for many years. I am aware of the reasons for the situation being as it is today, with the grain companies doing the cleaning with the facilities they have built at the ports, but it certainly seems to be one of the trends that has developed and that has not worked to the advantage of the western livestock industry.
With respect to livestock, the report sets out at page 277 two important principles. With respect to the economic development of the prairie region it states:
. . . the commission subscribes to the following principles:
(1)	The prairie region of Canada is basically an exporting region, and hence a
major contributor to Canada's favourable balance of payments position.
That is a point which needs to be stated and restated. The report goes on to read:
Current and future transportation policies should not detract from disposition but should recognize its importance in the national interest.
(2)	The production and processing of agricultural products should take place
in regions which enjoy natural locational advantages for such activities.
Freight rates and other transport related policies should not destroy these
natural locational advantages.
Again these are two points which certainly have the endor-sation of all the western members and, I am sure, of members from other parts of the country, on both sides of the House.
On the question of livestock and equity between the livestock and grain industries, we find the following statement in the report at page 309:
The commission recommends that freight rates on livestock and meat be set at levels which do not discriminate against the natural locational advantage of prairie livestock producers and processors.
Then the report goes on to discuss malting plants, flour milling and so on with respect to the processing of western products.
At page 336 of the report there is another reference to statutory freight rates, and we find this statement:
How the difference between the new rate and the Crowsnest rate will be apportioned between the government and the producer is, of course, a matter for government decision. This commission feels that the government must continue to subsidize the transportation of export grain and that the whole cost, as deemed by the commission on the costs of transporting grain by rail, must not be imposed on the producer.
That recommendation will have the support of western members in any party.
As to how it will be implemented to bring equity between the livestock and grain industries-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GRAIN HANDLING AND TRANSPORTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, together with other members of the House I am indeed eager and happy to take part in this debate on the Hall Commission report. Coming from a riding such as mine where perhaps 75 per cent of all the agricultural grain products are exported, the recommendations of the Hall Commission are very important to me.
As I mentioned previously the problem of the rationalization of the grain handling industry is very real. One has only to go to the Palliser wheat growers' conventions or other such conventions to realize that, in comparing the ability of Canadians and Americans to move grain in approximately the same conditions, most experts would say that we are probably ten years behind the Americans. While this does not necessarily impair our ability to export grain, until we make the necessary rationalization and expenditures, western farmers will be at a disadvantage in comparison with their American counterparts who are their main competitors, particularly in periods of good crops and high production and a depression on world markets, which is the case at present.
I would like to confine my remarks primarily to the port of Churchill as an added outlet for prairie grain. Although I believe the most important part of the report deals with rationalization, I must say that in my part of Manitoba the outline given by the Hall report seems to be particularly good.
The export of grain is vital to the farmers of western Canada, and there are really four main avenues by which the grain can be exported to the world. The first and oldest has been via Thunder Bay-Montreal and through the St. Lawrence ports and the port of Halifax. That route still takes 55 per cent of export grain.
Another main avenue has been through the west coast ports of Vancouver and Prince Rupert. There have been problems with the mountainous terrain, snowslides, and general congestion caused by superimposing on a system built some years ago the burden of a flow of grain that has become much larger due to the increase in trade with the Pacific Rim countries.

May 26, 1977
Hall Commission Report
A third route has been through Churchill, the oldest route by which trade reached the prairies from Europe. It is one that has not been exploited to its fullest.
The fourth route is to the south through the Mississippi River system. Many feel that perhaps that route would be the best, if not the cheapest, if politics had not cut off its use. I think a small amount of exports go that way; exports of flax, malting barley and, of course, more might go that way.
Events in Quebec have brought much more sharply into focus the possibility of exporting grain shipments through Churchill, should there be any change in the outlook in that province on the export of grain. Certainly the major grain companies have large installations on the St. Lawrence, but the premier of Quebec has indicated that he would attempt to use all the leverage possible to extract from the grain trade as high a toll as could be levied. He regards the St. Lawrence Seaway as being very important for his province in dealing with the rest of Canada with regard to trade and other problems.
The port of Churchill has never had a fair shake from the transportation autorities of Canada. It is obvious that transportation interests in Montreal have never wanted the port of Churchill to become an important shipping centre or to develop in even a modest way so that it might provide a reasonable alternative for the export of prairie grain, and one cannot particularly blame them for this.
Churchill was one of the first areas in western Canada which was a prominent base for Europeans. They established a port there in 1689, and a route from York Factory to Winnipeg flourished until the building of the Canadian Pacific Railway. It is to the credit of western farmers that they recognized early the great mileage that could be saved by the use of this route. It is closer, incidentally, than Thunder Bay is to most of the prairie region areas. The saving from Regina to Liverpool via Churchill is 1,000 miles over the Thunder Bay-Montreal route.
As early as 1885 expeditions were sent to investigate the building of a railroad, and finally Sir Wilfrid Laurier promised the Hudson Bay Railway. The railway from The Pas to Churchill, interrupted by the war, was started in 1911, and finally reached Churchill in 1929. The weight of the steel originally used was 80 pounds, but this was upgraded to 100 pounds, and work to upgrade this is expected to be finished by next year.
At Churchill the capacity of the grain terminal is five million bushels. Due to ice, the navigation season is restricted to approximately three months, from mid-July to mid-October. In recent years other bulk commodities such as sulphur have been added to the list of exports.
The proximity of the port of Churchill to the many producers of northern Manitoba and Saskatchewan has led prairie people to push for greater utilization of the port. Indeed for many producers the port of Churchill is not much more than half the distance to Thunder Bay. The Hudson Bay Route Association has been instrumental in promoting greater use of

Churchill, working, generally speaking, against the great indifference of the government, which is interested in preserving the port of Montreal.
The port of Churchill has certain disadvantages. One is that it is served only by the CNR and that there is no interchange of grain traffic to CP rail lines, although CP Rail is in the area. Studies undertaken by the two railways seem to indicate that there would be no savings brought about by the use of inter-rail exchanges. However, this seems to be doubtful, and one wonders if the railways conveniently found a way out because they were not interested in providing a true statement of what the situation was.
The Dominion Marine Association, based in Montreal, also strongly stated that the utilization of Churchill had reached its limit and that funds should be directed elsewhere to improve the efficiency of western Canadian grain shipments. However, I think they were definitely biased.
There are several pluses already going for the virtues of Churchill grain shipments. First, the CN rail line is in position and will soon be able to accommodate 100-ton hopper cars. Second, the Churchill terminal, with a five million bushel capacity, and almost as large as the largest anywhere in the country, is in good condition. However, it needs improved gallery belt capacity. In the 1976 season it handled 28 million bushels of grain, or a ratio of 6 to 1 in a three-month period. Improved technology could further eliminate the risk of ice. Furthermore, increases in Seaway tolls, or shipping disturbances in Montreal would make the Churchill route an attractive proposition.
Better sales planning by the Canadian Wheat Board and the filling of the terminal with clean grain would aid grain movements. Furthermore, the CP Rail study indicates that a saving of 762,000 loaded car miles over Thunder Bay is possible through interchanges, one at Tisdale and one at Yorkton, that is, interchanges between the CN and the CP.
There are some constraints. Cargo and haul insurance is still the same as that charged since 1956, even though technology has improved immensely since then. There are also constraints on the delivery system over the CNR, with the need for sidings on the Herchner and Thicket subdivisions, and a long track at Churchill. This would seem to indicate that with the use of hopper cars the rail capacity could be increased to 55 million bushels annually.
There was a great deal of dismay in western Canada when it was announced that the CN would not upgrade its work this year. That work had been planned for this part of the track. Obviously CN management, based in Montreal, has no concept of the needs of the western region, and I think CN did a great disservice to western Canadians when the management in Winnipeg was transferred to Montreal some years ago.
Furthermore, handling capacity could be increased by the use of pre-cleaned grain. The tight shipping schedule has limited the type and variety of grades to one or two. Also, some dredging and increased gallery conveyor capacity would accommodate considerably more use of the port of Churchill.
May 26, 1977

All of these are improvements which could be carried out with relatively small expenditure increases, when we consider some of the expenditures which are now undertaken. From the western Canadian point of view the administration set up-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the dinner recess I was about to mention the difficulties of the Port of Churchill having to make representations to the National Harbours Board through the same persons as those responsible for Montreal and Thunder Bay. Obviously Churchill will get short shrift.
The great port of Churchill which is very important to the autonomy and the independence and stability of exports of western Canadian grain, could also be used for sulphur, potash and other commodities. With the cost of transportation rising-and probably it will rise more steeply than other factors in the years to come-every effort must be made to ensure that our transportation resources are applied in the most effective and efficient manner. It should not be possible for the interests of the port of Montreal to hamper increases in transportation of grain that could be brought through the Churchill route.
Furthermore, the general feeling is that coal and other bulk products will overload the railway system in the next few years so that it may not be possible to ship all grain needed on the railway lines, at least when it is most opportune. Western premiers at their recent conference in Brandon called for the increased use of Churchill.
It seems important also that the provincial government of Manitoba, either by itself or in conjunction with the province of Saskatchewan, should proceed with the road to Churchill. The highway is already in place for much of the way. I understand that, from an engineering point of view, construction of the highway for the last 200 miles or so would be fairly easy.
The grain growing area, starting at The Pas in Manitoba and some of the Interlake country, would be less than 500 miles away, and when it is considered that trucking in the United States carries grain 800 to 1,000 miles in competition with the railways, a highway would make some good sense. Further, due to the long winter months and the freezing of the ground, the restraint factor on truck loads would not be nearly as great as it would be farther south. No doubt the shipping season at Churchill could be extended substantially. According to the most modest forecasts it could be increased 27 per cent. If icebreakers could be used, as in the St. Lawrence Seaway
Hall Commission Report
where the port of Montreal is, all year round, it seems likely that the shipping season could last six months.
The use of the port of Churchill has not been without its problems. CN rail lines have provided the port with its only rail service. This has meant that grain has been retained in northern Manitoba and north eastern Saskatchewan until the opening of the Churchill shipping season. The result has been that many farmers have been unable to deliver their quotas of grain until almost a year after their harvest and this has created hardships.
The Hall Commission seems to have worked out a logical solution to much of this problem. The idea of shipping precleaned grain to Churchill has much to commend it, and the use of Saskatoon and a new facility at Yorkton for carrying clean grain to Churchill would make a great deal of sense. It is estimated that the throughput of grain could be increased so that between 55 million and 60 million bushels could be put through with very little trouble.
The plan would also mean that CP rail blocks in the area would contribute to the total quantity of grain available for shipment. It is estimated that the area served would produce 240 million bushels so that, even if 60 million bushels were shipped from Churchill, the inconvenience of delayed quotas would be restricted. As well, the Saskatoon government terminal for cleaning grain is presently underutilized and the Hall Commission feels it could provide 30 million bushels of clean grain for Churchill during the season.
I am most intrigued by the possibility of Yorkton elevators providing another 30 million bushels of clean grain. It would have been nice to have the facility in Dauphin; I appreciate that that locality perhaps is not the most advantageous spot for it. Both railways would serve the Yorkton facility. In addition, the Hall Commission suggested that the use of screening in the general area of livestock feeding would be of advantage. The present situation has always seemed rather ridiculous. Dockage for which farmers are not paid is hauled to market and farmers are penalized for added weight. That is ridiculous.
I believe one of the factors militating against the enthusiastic use of Churchill has been this: if the grain handling companies send grain to Churchill, they deprive their terminals at Thunder Bay of revenue. Perhaps some way may be found whereby grain handling companies could have a share in the revenue accruing from the use of Churchill.
It also occurs to me that, instead of the Canadian government building the new elevator at Yorkton, one of the grain handling companies, private or co-operative, or even, hopefully, a consortium of both could build it. Although some resist hauling the grain long distances, many farmers would be happy to haul to a central terminal in Yorkton, say, particularly if the added efficiency of the handling system were compensated for in the prices received for haulage and convenience of delivery.

May 26, 1977
5988___________
Hall Commission Report
The use of Churchill is a symbol to the grain growers of the eastern prairies. Mr. McMillan, a farmer, had this to say at the annual meeting of the Hudson Bay Route Association:
If I am to increase my production, as I am being urged to do for moral and humanitarian reasons, and in the process, maintain a viable farm enterprise, it is essential that I have adequate port outlets to accommodate this increased tonnage. The Port of Churchill has the potential and strategic location to be such an export outlet.
A further indication of the thinking of many westerners on the value of the Churchill route can be noted in resolution 6, passed at the 33rd annual convention of the Hudson Bay Route Association held in Regina on June 21 and 22, 1976. It states:
Whereas a successful movement of 30 million bushels of grain through Churchill during the 1976 shipping season, could mean an extra 3 to 4'/2 million dollars for western grain producers and the western economy, and
Whereas the imposition and increase in tolls on the St. Lawrence Seaway soon to be imposed, will make the strategically located port of Churchill the most advantageous, competitive and rewarding eastward facing port for the export of western Canada grain.
Therefore be it resolved that this 1976 convention of the Hudson Bay Route Association go on record as requesting the Government of Canada, its agents, grain merchants and others involved to prepare and execute action to maximize grain shipments through Churchill over the longest possible season.
I hope the government will soon put that resolution into effect.

The right hon. gentleman from Prince Albert mentioned the railway to the north. It will not move much wheat for a year or two to Hay Lake. But you never know; it might. Really, I do not think Mr. Justice Hall went very far outside his terms of reference. He heard briefs from all oyer the prairies. Prairie people have always been interested in all parts of Canada and in developing Canada. No doubt some of them suggested building railways to the north, and no doubt Mr. Justice Hall examined the 13-volume study on that question.
No speaker opposite really dealt with the Prairie Rail Authority, or the 2,165 miles of track which is to be abandoned immediately. Nobody said that that was too much or not enough. I suppose, since 90 per cent of the track up for abandonment in the province of Alberta is in the constituency of Crowfoot, I could be excused for being vitally interested in the track which will be abandoned between the present and 1980. Actually, I am interested in the 2,344 miles of track which is to come under the Prairie Rail Authority. I wanted to hear the opposition speak on this. Is that enough track, or too much? Should the Prairie Rail Authority be a self-liquidating board? Should it go out of existence in 1990 as Mr. Justice Hall suggests? Should it have only a term life of some 12 years? The opposition does not know, although Mr. Justice Hall himself suggested that. The opposition has not directed its attention to that question. My opinion on that question is yes, it should have a term life. However, other speakers may express their views on this question.
Should that rail authority be a three-man board, as Mr. Justice Hall suggests, appointed by the federal government, or should some provinces have some representation on that board? It would have to be worked out with the provinces as to whether it should be other than a three-man board and whether there should be some provincial repesentation on it. Hall suggests that when a main track in the 2,300 miles is up for abandonment a provincial representative should sit in on those hearings as well as a municipal representative. You do not develop expertise in railroads in that way. You do not get a continuing knowledge being carried from one abandonment to the other. If that were the case, it would happen in the next 12 years with regard to the 2,344 miles. 1 do not think that is the best solution.
May 26, 1977

It would be better to have a larger board to start with, which has some provincial representation on it. I say that because much of the duties of the prairie rail authority will be to direct funds to either a highway, railway, railway maintenance or, as Hall says, the upgrading and rehabilitation of a railway track. It would be better to have knowledgeable people continue to sit on the board.
While the Hall Commission report is terrific and may well become the bible for prairie transport problems, it is not the absolute answer to all questions. It leaves many questions unanswered. I have mentioned a few with regard to the prairie rail authority.
I say to my friends in the Conservative party that the government does not have all the answers. We would like them to assist by offering suggestions rather going back to the year 1962.

speechtext:
The hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ritchie) referred to the port of Churchill. I concur in much of what he said in that regard. The Hall report suggests a terminal elevator at Yorkton to clean the grain. That is a good suggestion, one that is worthy of a great deal of study. I can assure prairie producers that the government will take a long hard look at that suggestion.
The suggestion that there be a CP hook-up for CP rail cars to go to Churchill is good. If any saving can be made in the transportation of grain, it should be looked at.
There has been no mention of the Hall report suggestion of a northern development authority in Alberta. That is a very novel idea. I believe it agrees with the thinking of the Alberta government. Therefore it is worthy of a great deal of merit.
I would like to see the northern development railway have a hook-up with the BC railroad. It should be used primarily to feed the Prince Rupert port which could then be used to greater extent.
The Hall report suggests a greater utilization of cars. His findings with regard to car utilization and the car cycle have been clearly evident for some time. The railroads, the government and the grain industry would welcome any constructive suggestions to speed up the car cycle. The cars sit on the railway track 25 per cent of the time empty, and 27 per cent of the time full. The report says that while they are sitting, they are not working. The complete cycle takes too long. The cars ought to be moving in some direction.
Hall Commission Report
The fundamental problem of getting grain into Vancouver has long been known to me and to many prairie people. There is a very interesting recommendation in the Hall report, at page 223. It deals with the Fraser River Bridge problem. It is owned by the government, but the controller of the traffic on that bridge is a despatcher out of Seattle. If what Hall says at page 223 is true, a lot of improvements could be made in that direction. It would improve the car utilization problem a great deal.
Mr. Hall dealt with the Crow rates. Many members spoke about them. Anyone who knows anything of my political history knows that I have defended them throughout the 19 years I have been in this House. 1 will, of course, continue to defend them.
The Hall report does not really give an answer with regard to what should be done about moving finished products. At page 309 he says they should move at the same rate, but he does not say how a railway should be provided with the revenue and what effect this will have on the finished products. At page 309 the report states:
The Commission recommends that freight rates on livestock and meat be set at levels which do not discriminate against the natural locational advantage of prairie livestock producers and processors.
What do the words "natural locational advantage" mean? How do you arrive at that? How do you maintain that? If the opposition has any solutions to offer to that problem, they would be welcomed on this side of the House.
The report refers to a terminal rail authority. However, Mr. Hall tends to reject the terminal rail authority, preferring a controller with power. There is really a very fine difference indeed. I would think that a permanent rail authority directing traffic into and out of Vancouver would have some power. A controller with power might well turn out to be a terminal rail authority. He really does not define how that power should be exercised, whether it would have authority over all commodities going into Vancouver, or just grain.
The report talks of a railway to the north, something that is particularly pleasing to me. The hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) and the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) agree on one thing at least, a railroad to the north. I find it interesting to see them agree on that.
There are many other questions that arise out of the Hall report. There is the whole question of the malting barley business and how to develop the processing business in western Canada without some kind of subsidy. The report does not go into that.
This is a very good report on railway problems in western Canada and on the movement of western Canadian goods to export markets. However, there are still many questions yet to be answered. I will be particularly pleased to help answer some of these problems when they come up.
I am pleased that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) has said that he is prepared to accept the abandonment of the 2,165 miles, and that the other 2,344 miles will be safeguarded

May 26, 1977
Hall Commission Report
until January, 1979. That gives the government ample time to discuss with the prairie governments the feasibility of setting up a Prairie Rail Authority, and whether that rail authority should handle the abandonment or upgrading of the 2,344 miles which Hall leaves in a state of limbo until 1990.
These questions will come up, for example, whether or not that rail authority should have the right to restrict the location of elevators along those lines. Some of the elevator companies are not too happy about that, and I note that members opposite have not given any clear expression of their views with regard to it. I believe the rail authority should have a great deal to say as to the location of these elevators on that 2,344 miles, but I have some reservations as to whether it should be the final authority.
In any case, I want to say that Mr. Hall has done western Canada a great service. He has produced a document which will enable the government to move forward with a transport policy which will greatly help the region. If we can iron out some of the difficulties which we see and which Mr. Hall sees, I believe the west will be well served.

to overcome the anomalies and inequities mentioned. But if we are to believe the words of the Minister without Portfolio there is really little hope that this will be the case. Speaking on that bill as a private member from this side of the House he said:
I believe this legislation takes the government from the mess it was in and puts it in another mess.
If that is an accurate description of this piece of legislation we really do not have much to look forward to.
If the government had fulfilled the commitments it made at the Western Economic Opportunities Conference the Commission's report would have been altogether different in terms of its contents and its recommendations. I believe very profoundly that if the major recommendations of the Hall report are implemented it could very well serve as a catalyst to propelling the west into its mature stage of economic development. This is why we on this side feel so strongly about this report and have brought it forth for debate. It is an important issue and we feel there should be no delay in the implementation of this report.
We believe there is a time for decision and a time for action, and that the action should take place here in the House of Commons. We do not need any more conferences, studies, task forces or other groups. We have had Snavely, Hall, and WEOC. The time has now come for action. It is not the responsibility of the opposition to initiate that action; it is the responsibility of the government to take action to implement the recommendations of the Hall report. I want to reinforce that contention as strongly as I can.
In his contribution to the debate this afternoon the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) made quite a political speech. He cited all the so-called good things which he has done for the west, and then he turned around and blamed the Conservatives for the fact that western Canada is mad at him. He spoke about a number of things, but he also omitted to mention a few others. He failed to mention the LIFT program. He failed to mention that his government followed a bible of agricultural policy known as the "Task Force Report on Agriculture," which was written by a group of economists, professors and accountants, and did not include one farmer. The major thrust of the agricultural policy of the former minister of agriculture came from that document. Out of it came the LIFT program, the stabilization program, and the marketing bill which caused a great deal of consternation across the country. The minister also failed to recognize that the second stabilization program which was brought in was a much improved version of the first one which he tried to ram through the House, attempting to buy off the western farmers using their own money in doing so.
The minister did say something positive and concrete, however. He announced that 1,813 miles of the 6,283 miles of line up for review will be transferred to the basic network, and that the freeze on 2,344 miles has been extended to January 1, 1979. We welcome that announcement.
We might ask, Mr. Speaker, why did we have a royal commission on this particular issue in the first place? The fact
Hall Commission Report
on the matter is that the commission was set up essentially to review and to sort out the 6,283 miles of branch line which were placed in the questionable category. The decision had to be made which lines should remain as part of the basic network and which lines should be abandoned. It was not an easy task. Because it was not an easy task and because it was an issue which was politically too hot to handle, the government decided to choose a royal commission to do the job. This royal commission has now brought forth its recommendations, among which is the recommendation that 2,165 miles of line be abandoned.
There is no question that the abandonment of these lines will cause a great deal of hardship to a number of communities and producers. There is no question that some areas have been dealt with rather harshly. But we have to recognize that rationalization on the part of the elevator and grain companies was taking place anyway, so that the blame cannot be laid solely upon the railways.
I am also concerned about the continuing uncertainty regarding the 2,344 miles of line which will be administered by the Prairie Rail Authority. Here too the grain companies will have a very large part to play in the success or failure of those particular lines.
Be that as it may, I think the commission approached this whole problem of abandonment in the most humane way possible. They tried to minimize the pain, distortion, and disruption which will take place as a result of the abandonment of these lines. The minister expresses concern about added costs. It should be pointed out that, as a result of the abandonment proposed by Mr. Justice Hall, elimination of these lines will result in a considerable saving to taxpayers. If I may quote from the Western Producer of May 19:
The elimination of some 2,160 miles of branch line railways in western Canada will save the Canadian taxpayers about $400 million, Chief Commissioner Emmett Hall told a May 16 press conference in Saskatoon following tabling of the grain handling and transportation commission report-
Rather significantly, the Western Producer goes on to say:
Regarding the federal government's proposal to build an additional 2,000 grain hopper cars at a cost of $80 million, Mr. Hall said while these may be needed some time in future, they are only "make work" projects for eastern industries and do not represent one additional dollar of revenue for western Canada.
We get the impression that it is all right to spend taxpayers' money in eastern and central Canada-the minister concurs with that-but he is very worried about subsidization of the Crow rate as it applies to western Canada. It is a very strange way for a minister from western Canada to react. More important, the report has come forth with some very positive proposals to improve and rationalize the grain handling and transportation system, a system which has deteriorated and become antiquated over the years. Certainly rationalization and improvement are long overdue.
Some will suggest that the commission went beyond its terms of reference. As a matter of fact the Minister without Portfolio, who has just spoken said he did not consider that the Hall commission went beyond its terms of reference. The Minister of Transport suggested that perhaps it did. Whatever

May 26, 1977
Hall Commission Report
opinion we choose to listen to, the fact of the matter is that as Canadians, and particularly as parliamentarians, we should be extremely grateful for the work Mr. Justice Hall and his fellow commissioners carried out. Unlike any other commission, this is probably the first time that we have had a grassroots opinion documented in such a comprehensive way. Perhaps it is the most democratic report ever documented. But because it is a grassroots report which has been prepared in the most democratic fashion possible is no reason why the report should be suppressed or smothered by politicians or bureaucrats.
In large measure the major contents of this report clash with present government policy. The report alludes to many important aspects of the grain trade, and furthermore it covers many important aspects of the potential economic future of western Canada. As has been pointed out previously, the report reaffirms the principle of statutory rates. I should like to place on the record a passage in the Hall commission report at page 545 which states this recommendation in very clear and concise terms:
The Commission recommends:
(1)	The retention of the Crow's Nest statutory rates.
Not the "statutory rates", Mr. Speaker, but the "Crowsnest statutory rates".
(2)	That the difference between the statutory rate and the cost of transporting grain be paid directly to the railways.
The wording is clear and concise and beyond question.
Secondly, what this report does is destroy what I refer to as the "Lang user-pay concept". I think it knocks that concept full of holes.
The report has exposed the failure of the Canadian Transport Commission to hold the railways responsible in the maintenance of their branch lines and in the administration of their subsidies. It has pointed out the fact that the Canadian Transport Commission has failed to compel the railways to carry out repairs and to provide the kind of service which was their responsiblity under the provisions of the Railway Act. It also points out that the Canadian Transport Commission refused to provide certain pertinent information to the commission. I think the minister should take a very close look at that because I believe the Canadian Transport Commission is not only compelled to provide this information, but it agreed to do so. That was a commitment which was made by the president of the Canadian Transport Commission before a committee of this House of Commons.
The Commission cites the failure of the railway to discharge its responsibilities. I would like to quote page 23 which reads as follows:
The Commission views with concern the action of the railway to render service in keeping with the convenience of the carrier rather than service as required by the public and in keeping with the intent of the laws of the land.
There is nothing new in that. It has been stated over and over again in this House and in committee. That is another area which needs some quick and serious attention. The Com-

mission confirmed the fact that transportation must be a tool for economic development. In my view, regional disparities will continue to grow, unless deliberate efforts are made to reduce them. One of the logical tools for achieving a reduction of those regional disparities is by providing a fair and equitable transportation system-efficient, effective and safe.
I want to emphasize the fact that the commission made specific reference to the treatment of the malting industry, the flour industry, the rapeseed industry, and the livestock processing industry. I am not going to quote the pertinent sections because at page 534 of the report it is clearly documented. In all cases the commission emphasized the fact that the production and processing of agricultural products should take place in the regions of this country which have a natural geographic advantage for such activities. It is rather odd that the Minister without Portfolio finds that unclear. It simply points out that if you are going to process rapeseed in Canada it should be processed where it is grown. That is what Mr. Hall was saying. He is suggesting the same thing with the flour industry and the same thing with the malting industry.
I am not sure what the minister intends to do with one particular recommendation. Perhaps it is an area that can be considered by the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications. I am referring to the very important recommendation having regard to the Prairie Rail Authority. This body will be a very important mechanism in determining the future of the 2,344 miles which are still under review- whether they will fall into one class or another. The unfortunate part of the 2,344 miles is the fact that there will be a period of uncertainty as to whether the line will stay or whether it will go. As the minister who spoke before me indicated, it may very well be logical to establish a prairie rail authority which has continuing powers similar to the CTC.

Mr. Speaker, I shall not abuse the courtesy of the House. I appreciate being given the opportunity to conclude my remarks.
The recommendations having regard to the improved rail car utilization are very valid and could be acted upon very quickly. Utilization of the inland government terminals is certainly a very valid and worthy consideration. A controller with power, as described at page 222, is another important consideration. An improved co-ordination of the rail operation in the port of Vancouver, which has become a serious bottleneck, is another important consideration.
The commission points out that railways must be compensated for delivering reasonable service, but in turn the railways must accept their responsibility in ensuring that service is provided with all reasonable dispatch; that lines are maintained and upgraded in a safe and functioning condition; and
May 26, 1977

that the basic infrastructure remains solid and on a good foundation. This is certainly an area we must act upon because most of us who come from western ridings will realize railways have not discharged their responsibilities as they are obligated to do under the provisions of the Railway Act. Someone must be in a position of authority to ensure that that service is carried out on behalf of the western farmers, and indeed on behalf of all Canadians.
In summary, this report in many ways highlights the failure of the government to come up with feasible and equitable policies for western Canada to achieve its legitimate aspirations. The report suggests, and in fact may even demand, that it is time we in this House realize it is the responsibility of the government to take the initiative. I am sure it will find support on this side. It is time the government recognized the shortcomings which have plagued western Canadians and set out to establish and proclaim a new industrial strategy for western Canada based upon the recommendations of the Hall Report.
Mr. Speaker, we have the report. It is the responsibility and the duty of the government to respond, to act, and to do this without political motivations. I would hope it would do this as required and not simply for political maximization. It is time for decision. The report should not be allowed to gather dust. The government must not procrastinate. It is a grass roots report. The Commission has patiently and diligently sought out all those who wanted to be heard, and now it is the duty of the government to act. I am sure if it acts it will find this side of the House will support it in overcoming the barriers, the inequities, the discriminations, and the shortcomings of the transportation system which is so vitally important to the future and the economic lifeblood of western Canada.
