speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GRAIN HANDLING AND TRANSPORTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the report of the commission headed by Mr. Justice Hall dealing with grain and rail in western Canada is similar to the earlier report of the commission headed by Mr. Justice Hall which dealt with health services. The report's recommendations will play an important role in the life of western Canada for generations to come.
We in the New Democratic Party support the basic principles which Mr. Justice Hall and his commission recommended. That is why we support the motion put down by the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker). Realizing the complexity of the many recommendations made by the Commission, we have singled out three particular aspects of the recommendations: first, that the Crowsnest rates be maintained; second, that the principle of the Crowsnest rates be extended to agricultural products processed in western Canada; third, that the utilization of the ports of Churchill and Prince Rupert be increased.
I believe that the Hall Commission has laid down a new socio-economic charter for western Canada. It has told both the federal government and the railways what their respon-
Hall Commission Report
sibilities are and what is required to redress the wrongs which have been done to western Canada over almost a century. What has the Commission said? It has said that it wants the retention and even the expansion of the Crowsnest freight rate. I know that there are some members of the House, and certainly many people in Canada, who do not know what the Crowsnest agreement was. So, for their information, let me summarize what that agreement says.
The agreement, made in 1897 between the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Government of Canada, had three main provisions. First, the company agreed to build a railway line from Lethbridge to Nelson, B.C., crossing the Rockies through the Crowsnest pass. Second, the government agreed to subsidize the line to the extent of $11,000 per mile, which worked out to a total of $3,400,000. Third, the company agreed to reduce freight rates on certain specified commodities between eastern and western Canada, the most important of which were grain and flour eastbound to the lakehead for export and farm implements westbound to the prairies. In return, the company received a land subsidy from the government of B.C. for building part of the line, and the deal with Ottawa made it possible for CPR to take advantage of that deal. The CPR estimated before the MacPherson Commission some years ago that the revenue it received from Cominco, which was on land which the CPR got as a result of that deal since Cominco was formed as a company in 1906, amounted to almost $250 million. If you calculate what they have taken in since then, you arrive at a figure of over $350 million.
So anybody who thinks that the CPR got taken is, of course, completely wrong, and we see no reason why the CPR, having made a deal from which they did very well at the expense of the people of Canada, should not be required to continue with that deal. We think, therefore, it is reasonable that the statutory rates be continued. My colleague, the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom), dealt with that earlier this afternoon.
The commission also said that the responsibility for the future use of prairie rail lines should be taken away from the railways and the Ottawa based Canadian Transport Commission and given to a separate prairie based organization. We support that. We have been, to say the least, critical of the somewhat incestuous relationship which we believe has continued for far too long between the railways and the CTC.
Lastly, the Commission recommended that western Canada get a better opportunity to diversify and expand its economic base. I want to spend most of the time which I have left dealing with that last recommendation, but before I do that I think we should get something clear. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) and the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Horner) have spoken about how they agree with the recommendations made by Mr. Justice Hall. It is pretty obvious, as one reads the report and its recommendations, that the commission is against the user-pay transportation policy which has been enunciated and argued for by the Minister of Transport since he took over that portfolio. The commission is saying that grain is such an essential key to the country's future

May 26, 1977
(2110)
Hall Commission Report
prosperity that its transportation must be subsidized by the people of Canada as a whole.
It is interesting to compare the recommendations of the Hall Commission with the recommendations made by the four western premiers, coming from different political parties, which they made after the Western Economic Opportunities Conference a few years ago. Those recommendations, despite early endorsement by the then minister of transport who said publicly that transportation in Canada was a mess, have been almost completely ignored by the present Minister of Transport and the government. I think it is ludicrous for the Minister of Transport to be saying now that he accepts the recommendations of the Hall Commission when in fact he has been ignoring those same recommendations which have been made by the western premiers.
As I said, I want to deal in the main with one aspect of the recommendations made by the Hall Commission, that is, the recommendations made in the field of economic development. The key recommendation is summarized in Mr. Justice Hall's report on page 277, and I want to read just the paragraph in which he summarizes the principle in which he believes and which he recommends. Then I want to give some of the reasons and some illustrations of why he came to the conclusion which he did. This is what he said at page 277 of the report:
(2) The production and processing of agricultural products should take place in regions which enjoy natural locational advantages for such activities. Freight rates and other transport related policies should not destroy these natural locational advantages.
It is not surprising to me that in a country as large in geography as Canada ministers of transport who were elected from other regions of Canada, particularly those who came from Ontario or Quebec, should not understand the needs of western Canada or indeed of Atlantic Canada, and should not promote policies which would be helpful and advantageous to western Canada. But it constantly amazes me how this Minister of Transport, coming as he does from the province of Saskatchewan, should have consistently, and almost from the day on which he took office as Minister of Transport, enunciated and put forward policies which have been and are detrimental to western Canada. One needs only to read quickly through this chapter of the Hall Commission report on economic development and to compare what he says with what the minister has been doing to see how correct I am in what I am saying.
Mr. Hall pointed out that an analysis of the freight rate structure confirms that the prairie provinces have been victimized by discriminatory freight rates from the beginning. It goes on in this chapter to show in detail how that discrimination has continued right until today. He says:
Since early development the thrust has been to move raw materials to industrial central Canada for refinement and consumption ...
The continuous shift of an ever increasing proportion of the population to urban central Canada has been aggravated by the retention of policies which favour maintaining the west as a source of raw goods, and carrying out processing next to the populous centres of the east.

That population drift has continued for generations in western Canada, certainly in the three prairie provinces, with the exception of the period since the discovery of major oil and gas in the province of Alberta. It has continued at a slower or faster rate in the last 25 or 30 years regardless of what parties formed the governments of the provinces of Manitoba and Saskatchewan. In the last couple of years there has been a slight increase in population in each of these provinces, but in fact we have had a continuous movement out of Saskatchewan and Manitoba because of this discrimination against the west with regard to freight rates.
Mr. Justice Hall found that the application of certain government programs, Canadian Wheat Board selling practices and ancillary rate charges have offset the natural geographic advantage which western flour mills should enjoy. One of the natural or locational advantages of locating a flour mill near the source of wheat is the reduced need for storage, Mr. Justice Hall points out, yet despite that the flour milling industry has increasingly been located in eastern Canada. So the commission recommends that the flour milling industry in Canada be permitted to enjoy the natural geographic advantage of locating in western Canada.
The Commission also recommends that railway policies and Wheat Board policies which discriminate against western Canada be discontinued. The Commission was referring to policies which have been continued all during the time that the present Minister of Transport has been in office.
Then the Commission goes on to analyze what has happened with regard to the processing of rapeseed. At page 287 of the Commission's report we learn that the cost of moving 100 pounds of rapeseed from Lethbridge to Montreal is 70.5 cents per hundred pounds and that the cost of moving the equivalent amount of oil and meal is calculated to be 90.2 cents. This difference of 19.7 cents makes it advantageous to move the rapeseed before it is processed. I could go on and on. The Commission recommends that freight rates on rapeseed and its derivatives be set at levels which do not discriminate against the natural locational advantage of prairie rapeseed crushers.
Then the Commission deals with the question of livestock and with the subsidies on moving feed grain. It points out that the feed grain assistance program has consistently been to the advantage of eastern Canada and British Columbia and against the interests of prairie grain producers. It points out that transport subsidies such as the feed grain assistance program encourage the shipment of feed grains rather than livestock or livestock products from the prairies to eastern Canada and British Columbia. That is what Mr. Justice Hall was talking about when he suggested that the processing of agricultural products be encouraged to develop near where the agricultural products are grown.
Then the Commission talks about the shipment of livestock and the advantages of shipping live cattle compared with the disadvantage to western Canada of first processing the meat.
May 26, 1977

Then the Commission goes into the question of the malting industry, and it recommends that the malting industry be permitted to enjoy the natural geographic advantage of locating in prairie Canada.
What Mr. Justice Hall says in this report is what western Canadians from all parties have been saying for more than 50 years. Western Canadians do not want to be subsidized by other areas. Western Canada has resources; it can produce a great deal more than it has been producing. Its people can live well with the resources they have. Western Canada cannot develop if the Government of Canada adopts policies which help move raw materials to central Canada for processing.
Mr. Justice Hall has laid down a policy which I think all western Canadians, regardless of where they live and regardless of what party they belong to, can support, and they will expect the government to implement that policy.
It may be that the Minister of Transport really means it when he says he accepts and supports the basic proposals made by Mr. Justice Hall in his report. As I have said, I find that difficult to believe because everything Mr. Justice Hall has recommended the minister has been working against since he became the minister. However, I accept his statement that he accepts the basic recommendations in the report. I hope and expect that he has really changed his mind and that, having read the report, he realizes that the recommendations are indeed worth-while, that they will improve the conditions of life for people in western Canada, and that he will implement those recommendations. To the extent that he does he will have the support of members of the New Democratic Party in parliament. To the extent that he fails we will continue to criticize him and to point out the differences between what he is doing and what he says he will do, and we will continue to urge him and the government to implement the report of the Commission, which the government in fact appointed.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GRAIN HANDLING AND TRANSPORTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased indeed to have this brief opportunity to participate in this debate. 1 want to say at the outset that I was very impressed with the possibility of favourable response as outlined by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) in his clear exposition of the situation as it now exists after the Hall report. I was also impressed with the statesmanlike character of the remarks made by the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Horner) and with the constructive remarks of the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski), both of which I found extremely interesting because I think we have passed the stage of dealing with freight rates and questions of that kind in terms of rhetoric, and in this House this evening and today we were getting down to practical specifics and a willingness to deal with these questions as they ought to have been dealt with for some time. But we now have more knowledge.
Many in this House are far more qualified than 1 am to discuss the specifics of the Hall recommendations. I tend to think that the recommendation of a Prairie Rail Authority is an appropriate one, but I do not profess to have been able to study these questions in depth.
Hall Commission Report
Over the past six months I have had the opportunity to attend a number of conferences in western Canada. 1 attended a series of conferences known as the Meat-Grain Interface Conferences, and at those conferences 1 came to realize how complex indeed are the interwoven factors of transportation, processing, community development and so forth. Those conferences, sponsored by the University of Saskatchewan in Saskatoon under Professor Red Williams and Professor Grant Devine, were an eye opener for me, and 1 wish more people could have attended them.
I thought it might be useful for someone from central Canada to make a few remarks about the attitude with which people in Ontario and Quebec will approach the questions that the Hall Commission raises. I think it is true that, as the hon. member for Vegreville said, we too want action. We are fatigued with the rhetoric that we have heard for so long about discrimination and victimization. To the extent it exists, we want to see an end to it.
I think it is fair to say that in Ontario and Quebec there has never been a time when there was a more positive attitude toward prairie economic development and the resolution of these grievances. I personally am very pleased that the Hall Commission considered the social and community aspects whether of abandonment of rail lines or of the consolidation of elevator systems. I think we in Ontario and Quebec, and indeed in the rest of Canada, understand what is going on in the minds of people in the prairie provinces. After all, it was people from Ontario and Quebec who went west 75 years ago to build that region. They are ready now to face the developmental needs of the second wave, which 1 take to be not only reorganization and rehabilitation but development in the sense of industrialism. People came also from all over the world to the prairie region. They built it and became Canadians, settling along those branch lines, hauling grain to those elevators, many of which are now old and need rebuilding. Many of the branch lines also require expensive rehabilitation as a result of lack of maintenance.
I recall Mr. Snavely, the commissioner who looked into the cost of moving grain in the west, saying in an aside, not in his report, that in a few years trains would be derailed, standing still on those branch lines. We appreciate the need for rehabilitation.
I want to say again that I think the time for rhetoric is past but we want to make sure in very specific terms what is required and what would be useful. It seems to me that after WEOC meetings four years ago there was a decided cooling of the rhetoric. After WEOC there was full disclosure to the provinces of railway costs. There was a systematic attempt to look into those grievances which are simply referred to as freight rates by many. When one gets down to specifics, for example, the movement of rapeseed oil to Vancouver, or the anomalies between the short-haul and the long-haul charges, or the discrimination apparent between the costs of moving raw material and finished goods-when one gets past the

May 26, 1977
Hall Commission Report
generalities as was done after WEOC, then it is very hard to document specific cases in proof of discrimination. I think we therefore feel cautious about a generalized approach that is not worked out in specific detail so that, after what might appear to have been a response, those grievances were still there as if untouched.
1 suggest we should deal with the Commission report on the merits of its recommendations but enlarge the context into a social and economic developmental approach to the prairie region. By doing that we will go beyond transportation and be obliged to bring in the Department of Regional Economic Development and the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, and we will be obliged to consider the trade initiatives that ought to be taken, for example, to sell meat in Japan, or in the Pacific northwest, and the tariff negotiations that will be required to sell polyvinyl chloride in the United States. We will be compelled to go beyond transportation because, unless we do we will not resolve the problems.
We may well need massive freight rate changes, rail rehabilitation, a remodelled grain handling system, new port facilities, and better labour-management relations at the ports throughout the system. Yet these things will not be enough as they are only one set of elements in the total developmental package needed for the prairie region.
What we require and are ready for now is a selective development strategy to undertake all of the best recommendations in the Hall report and reinforce it with policies setting a taxation environment for the prairie region, policies for DREE, as well as tariff changes and redirected government procurement policies. We need this plus greater assurance of markets in central Canada for the processed products of the west even as the west was an assured market through national policies for the manufactured products made in the central industrial heartland.
What we need therefore is an industrial policy which starts with the strengths of the prairie region, which starts with the primary manufacturing already based there on the existing resources, and find the policies which will aid that manufacturing to integrate backwards and forwards as it were-to integrate backwards to include more of regional inputs into the manufacturing process-to make compressors for example for the pipelines-and forward integration as well to make more and more end products as one goes down the processing stream. Those policies will not be easy to find or effect.
Reading the Hall Commission report I feel that the references to natural geographical advantages, or locational advantages as the hon. Minister without Portfolio put it, are not clearly defined and ought not to mislead us. There are very strong economic advantages to processing near the market. They are stronger than the economic advantages of processing near the raw material. Thus it will not be enough simply to change freight rates or change the transportation system. It will require a complete mix of development policies and a long-term convergence of those policies, together with the will to maintain them until these primary manufacturing industries

can move up the economic chain into further processing. It will require a good deal of inter-regional understanding.
The main point I am trying to make is that such regional understanding is already there so far as central Canada is concerned. We too want, as the hon. member for Vegreville said, a charter for western economic development. We too want to see a "way ahead" for the prairie region. Mr. Justice Hall and his commissioners have set us on course with this report.
In conclusion, I suggest that if I am right about the need for something more comprehensive than freight rates, better elevators and rehabilitated grain lines, all of which one accepts, we will need at the federal level some means to co-ordinate our responses, some means to go beyond the Department of Transport and include all other departments of government which have a vital role to play in that economic package. I am thinking of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, the Department of Agriculture which has a central role to play, the Department of Finance, and so on. Do we not need to set up a task force? Let us not be blase about task forces. There must be a mechanism for co-ordinating the federal approach.
Second, we need a commitment from the federal government, which I am sure will not be difficult to get, that it will sit down with the three prairie provinces, and with each separately within the next few weeks, and seek to identify specific recommendations in the Hall Commission report which could be usefully implemented with early action.
Mr. Speaker, I have made my few points. I have tried to talk constructively in this debate about the real opportunity existing in the prairie region for dynamic economic development. This opportunity comes, oddly enough, at the very time when the dynamism of central Canada is perhaps declining. Central Canada therefore needs the development of the prairie provinces now more than it may have needed it in the past. Constructive responses to this shift in economic vocations, futures or possibilities, may indeed involve us in the very unifying activities into which we all now want to enter.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GRAIN HANDLING AND TRANSPORTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will begin by saying this is a timely debate for western agriculture, western Canada and, indeed all Canada. I was privileged to present a personal brief in my Medicine Hat constituency at the hearing held in Schuler, Alberta, on March 23, 1976. Schuler is a small Alberta town, very close to the Alberta-Sas-katchewan border, and about 40 miles northeast of Medicine Hat. The town is located at the end of a branch line to a branch line which runs to a third branch line.
To me one of the highlights of that particular hearing, and 1 am sure to the Schuler community, was that all high school students were given the day off to attend this particular hearing, which was conducted by commissioners Reiny Lehr and Bob Cowan. I point out that Mr. Lehr is a near resident to
May 26, 1977

Schuler and Medicine Hat, where he produces grain and cattle.
It seems to me that there is, and should be, broad general support for the recommendation dealing with the abandonment within five years of some 2,165 miles of branch lines. Though there may be a few cases of inconvenience on these lines owing to abandonment, the need for such action seems both apparent and necessary. One such example is a 21-mile rail line from near Cardston to Whiskey Gap, in South-Western Alberta. It serves four elevators at only two points. Incidentally, it is interesting to note that the original line was built initially by the St. Mary's River Railway as a narrow gauge railway; later the line was taken over by the CPR. I also single out the Bassano to Leader line, which it was recommended should be added to the basic network. I concur with this recommendation, since it is part of an important alternate rail route to the main CPR line connecting Swift Current and Bassano, Alberta.
My remarks today will be specifically directed to the sections in the Hall report on statutory rates and economic development.
With respect to the question of the Crowsnest rates and/or statutory rates, and I think those terms are often used interchangeably, it seems quite probable that after the conclusion of public hearings and just before writing the report, the six commissioners must have agreed at the outset that the Crowsnest rates were too touchy a political issue and changes should not be suggested. They responded accordingly and built the remainder of their recommendations on this base, that the Crowsnest rates should remain. Having been a member of this House over four and a half years I can now understand this approach. At one time I might not have fully understood it. It also seems probable that most of the representations made to the commission hearings must have indicated a similar response.
Let us look at the actual recommendations of the report of this item. I am referring to pages 336 and 337 of the report. It states:
Regardless of what rate may be set for the transport of grain to export position that rate must be statutory, not variable. Anything else would be a violation of promises made to the producers of western Canada. If the government considers that the railways should have the amount suggested by the Commission on the Costs of Transporting Grain by Rail to transport grain, that amount, according to the findings of that Commission, will be in excess of the Crowsnest rate. How the difference between the new rate and the Crowsnest rate will be apportioned between the government and the producer is, of course, a matter for government decision. This Commission feels that the government must continue to subsidize the transportation of export grain and that the full cost, as deemed by the Commission on the costs of transporting grain by rail, must not be imposed on the producer.
The Commission goes on to make the following recommendation:
The Commission recommends that the difference between the Crowsnest rate and the rate determined through costs found by the Commission on the Costs of Transporting Grain by Rail should be paid directly to the railways, and not to individual farmers. The very idea of sending out cheques to 160,000 farmers is appalling.
Hall Commission Report
Please note the specific recommendation for payments made to railways not to farmers. Also note that in the passage quoted the phrase "export grain" is used twice when grain is referred to. I can only assume that this recommendation includes domestic feed grains which move by rail in western Canada, because this is the case now.
I now turn to pages 534, 535 and 536 of the report, to that part entitled economic development. It relates specifically to four agricultural processing industries, all directly involved in prairie grain production. I draw your attention, Mr. Speaker, to the four similar statements which follow a more general opening statement. I quote:
The production and processing of agricultural products should take place in the regions of this country which have a natural geographic advantage for such activities.
With respect to the flour milling industry the Commission recommends that the flour milling industry in Canada be permitted to enjoy the natural geographic advantage of locating in western Canada.
With respect to the rapeseed crushing industry the Commission recommends that freight rates on rapeseed and its derivatives be set at levels which do not discriminate against the natural locational advantage of prairie rapeseed crushers.
With respect to the livestock processing industry the Commission recommends that freight rates on livestock and meat be set at levels which do not discriminate against the natural locational advantage of prairie livestock producers and processors.
Finally, with respect to the malting industry the Commission recommends that the malting industry be permitted to enjoy the natural geographic advantage of locating in prairie Canada.
I suggest these four statements are deliberately vague and leave much to conjecture as to how these statements are to be implemented. My personal impression is that there is a clear indication in these statements that statutory rates should apply not only to domestic feed grains, but to products of domestic feed grains as well. These products are flour, rapeseed and rapeseed oil, livestock and meat, and barley malt.
By obvious implication, the report also suggests that the difference between statutory and compensatory rates be made up by government for all commodities and processed agricultural products from the prairies.
I suggest that if these assumptions are correct, there are some very serious consequences that until now have hardly even been mentioned. I will name only a few. What would these changes in rail freight do to the trucking industry? How would our two way agricultural trade with the United States be affected? Of course, there is the obvious question of what these costs will come to, including the cost of extending statutory rates to all sectors of agriculture in the west. The future of western Canada's feeding industry, especially cattle feeding, could be very well decided by how these questions are
5998

May 26, 1977
Hall Commission Report
answered and what policies are evolved for our domestic feed grain industry.
The west's feeding industry for both cattle and hogs is in serious trouble now because of two factors relating to freight rates. First, statutory rates now tend to increase the western domestic price of feed grains by the difference between the costs of statutory and actual rail costs by about 27 cents a bushel. Second, cattle and beef, hogs and pork are at the full compensatory rate when moved by rail.
The results of these two factors were almost predictable. Our western hog industry has shifted to the United States. We have seen a drop of about 40 per cent since 1941 and a near corresponding increase in Quebec, but the shift is really to the United States. We are now importing pork in substantial quantities from the United States.
Western cattle feeding could be headed the same way. This spring for the first time in years significant numbers of feeder cattle are moving south to the United States from western Canada and we can expect fat cattle to flow back north from the U.S. corn belt into central Canada, probably this fall or next winter. What a tremendous loss there is here in value added enterprises.
How can the natural comparative advantages, or as the report says the natural locational advantages, be assured for those value added agricultural industries like livestock and meat processing? To suggest a partial answer, let us go back to the recommendation that the difference between Crow and actual cost of moving grain be paid to the railways. I suggest this will continue to distort the natural comparative advantage of western value added industries. If such a subsidy is to be used, let it be paid directly to grain producers on an acreage base, not a bushel base. Existing permit books could be used quite readily for this purpose. I quote the Commission's comment or reason for not doing this:
The very idea of sending out cheques to 160,000 farmers is appalling.
It just does not make sense in this computer age when millions of cheques are being sent out, such as initial and final wheat board cheques. Direct payment of the difference to grain producers would eliminate that price inequity on domestic feed grains in the west, but payment to the railways would merely continue this inequity on western feed grains.
If this suggestion relative to the Hall recommendation on who should receive the subsidy cannot be agreed to by the government and parliament, all I can say is that there has to be some other way devised to return the benefits of the Crow rate to grain farmers, particularly domestic feed grain farmers, in order to remove price distortion from the market.
Cattle and hog feeders in no way want to eliminate the Crow benefits to grain producers. They are simply suggesting that these benefits be returned in some other neutral manner. Western Canada does indeed have a natural locational advantage, not only for wheat production but feed grain production, especially barley.
Western barley production is a big crop every year, usually around 500 million bushels. It is disbursed as follows: 200

million bushels are exported, 66 million shipped to central and eastern Canada and British Columbia, and the balance, the biggest amount, fed in the west. Not mentioned there is the barley produced on a farm and fed on that farm, and never goes to a market as grain.
The point I want to emphasize is that our western market for barley is our most important market, and it is right at our front and back door. Ways must be found, either through recommendations by Hall or by parliament, to ensure that this domestic market has a chance to operate in a proper natural advantageous climate.
There is a noticeable sense of expectation in the west now that is linked to the Hall Commission report. While there are many important details missing from the report, the opportunity is now here for parliament to bring about meaningful solutions to grain marketing and rail transportation problems for the first time this century. It is up to us to act now.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GRAIN HANDLING AND TRANSPORTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this has certainly been a momentous day for Canada. We have heard much of the debate as it has taken place. The Hall report is a tremendous report for western Canada. As many westerners would say, and as my good friend opposite has said, when any one section of the country has increased in its strength, the whole country reaps the advantage.
I was pleased, as was my colleague who just spoke, to attend a local hearing when the Hall Commission was meeting. I attended a hearing in Stettler, Alberta. I spoke principally in terms of the importance of the prairie community system and the importance of the railway to that community system.
Because time is running short this evening, and there will be far more comments to be made than one opposition day will allow, or the short ten minutes I will have to speak this evening, I want to get to the heart of what the previous speaker has said, the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave).
The motion put before the House today reads:
That this House agrees in principle with the recommendations of the Hall Commission on Grain Handling and Transportation.
Those general principles of agreement go without any question. However, we must take a sincere look at specific aspects of that recommendation because there is still, depending upon interpretation, the possibility for great jeopardy to western Canada.
I want to put forward one submission on some advantages and disadvantages, to the prairies. I quote from a gentleman in the beef industry in a very big way, Mr. Chris Mills, as follows:
"It virtually spells the end of the livestock feeding business in western Canada. Within five years the cattle industry will go the same way as the hog feeding industry has in the last two years," he said of the Hall Commission's recommendation that the Crowsnest rate be retained.
We are not talking simply about the retention of the Crowsnest Pass rates but also about the methodology. There is no question in anyone's mind that these rates are the Magna
May 26, 1977

Carta of western Canada, part of the way in which we are linked together. The whole rail system on the prairies is as vital to national unity in the eyes of the west as other aspects may be to different parts of the country.
I cannot help noting considerable opposition to the position taken by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang). We note a headline in one of the papers, "Lang Upset." The report says:
Lang contended the commission's conclusion is unsubstantiated. He said the implied suggestion by the Commission that freight rates on processed commodities be brought into line with the current export grain rates would be a "very, very expensive solution."
I should like to remind hon. members of what Commissioner Emmett Hall stated in response to the argument put forward by the Minister of Transport. He said, and I am quoting:
I reject it in grain transportation because I consider grain so fundamental to the fiscal well-being of Canada that the national interest does not justify the user pay principle.
The Minister of Transport is quite willing to take the position that the recommendation is too expensive for Canada. But Mr. Emmett Hall has pointed out that grain exports have consistently, over the years, reduced the deficit in Canada's balance of payments. In other words, it was a great national advantage, not just a western advantage, and to think of this, in the words of the Minister of Transport as being a western issue rather than a national issue is to fail to understand where Canada starts or ends. It is a great shortcoming that the minister does not see this question in its international context. As Emmett Hall stated:
The contribution which grain makes to Canada's balance of payments position demands that a substantial part of any increase be borne by the federal government in the national interest.
I want to speak this evening about the "order-in-council government" we have at the present time, a government which has issued more than 3,000 orders-in-council during the past year. Speaking on this motion, the Minister of Transport told us earlier that the government had today put out yet another order-in-council. A couple of days ago an order-in-council was issued dealing with the Hall report. What makes me nervous about these orders-in-council is that they make an impression that the government is actually doing something, that it is implementing the Hall recommendations, while in fact it is not. By acting in this way it fails to give the prairie system the solid feeling of security which will come from parliament taking action by statute, passing legislation which could not be changed at the whim of ministers-any change would have to be made subject to public debate.
I deplore the fact that we are moving by order-in-council in the absence of the kind of debate on this subject in which we ought to be engaged. If the minister were really sincere about implementing these recommendations by order-in-council he might take some of the more fundamental recommendations of the report, such as the following:
The retention of the Crowsnest statutory rates. That the difference between the statutory rate and the cost of transporting grain be paid directly to the railways.
He might have considered enacting that by order-in-council. I am not suggestion he should, though. What I am saying is
Hall Commission Report
that this is not a new debate. As my right hon. friend from Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) said, it has been going on for 50 years.
Had the government followed the recommendations of the Western Economic Opportunities Conference in 1973, the Hall Commission would not have been required. That conference put forward a manifesto for the west giving the kind of guarantees we are seeking here today. All that we are asking, and all that the report purports to do, is to give the prairies the same kind of natural economic advantages which are enjoyed and exercised by other parts of the country.
In its recommendations with regard to the rationalization of the grain handling system the report mentions the fact that at the present time five major government-built inland terminals are empty and unused. On our side we recognize there is a need for the rationalization of the system in order to make it efficient. We do not need another study.
The Minister of Transport told us today that studies have been going on since 1968. He went on to list ad infinitum the studies which have been conducted over the years. The people of the prairies do not want to hear of another study. One of the things we know about this report, even though we agree with it, or at least with its major principles, is that it offers nothing new, nothing which the farmers, the small businessmen, the industrialists, have not been saying in the western provinces over the years. Today we have trains which chase east to haul grain west, which chase north to haul grain south, all because we lack a rational system of train exchange on different tracks. I have in my constituency a line which must carry grain a hundred miles to the east before turning around and bringing it west again to Vancouver. That is a nonsensical situation, to say the least.
One of the fundamental things this report does is give fair warning to the government that it had better not plan to call an election before implementing some of these vital recommendations. If the government were to dare to call an election without acting on this report after 50 years of protest by the prairie farmers, it would be a snub to the people of the west. As for the Minister of Transport, I am not in any way persuaded that he is giving a full or firm commitment. That ought to be underscored.
We also need to take a look at the fact that in east central Alberta and west central Saskatchewan grain is shipped to Thunder Bay when ports have been frozen up during the past winter, as they are each winter. It is a nonsensical position if they do not empty the prairie elevators in the fall of the year and have the terminals at Thunder Bay emptied also. The minister today sought to leave the impression that there had been an improvement in the movement of grain under his administration. The fact of the matter is that in east central Alberta and western Saskatchewan there has been the highest congestion on both tracks ever experienced in recent years as a result of ill-conceived policy.
I see you are about to rise, Mr. Speaker, and call it ten o'clock. I just want to make it clear that it is the time which
6000

May 26, 1977
Adjournment Debate
has run out, not the issues, and that there is a lot more to be said about this subject.

subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-REQUEST FOR EQUIPMENT TO ASSIST RESIDENTS OF COBALT FOLLOWING FIRE
NATIONAL DEFENCE-REQUEST FOR EQUIPMENT TO ASSIST RESIDENTS OF COBALT FOLLOWING FIRE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Monday of last week a catastrophe happened to the people of the town of Cobalt. Most people know Cobalt as a small mining community in northern Ontario. It is surprising how many people have come to know the town of Cobalt over the years. Very few people you meet have failed to hear of that small community. At one time it consisted of 20,000 people, but has now quietly dwindled to a town with about 2,000 residents who are very devoted to the community and proud of the efforts they have made to maintain it over the years in the face of great adversity.
The fire that struck Cobalt last week was a disaster. It started in a building which was being torn down, and with a 60 miles an hour wind it spread rapidly to other parts of the town. As many as five or six houses were burning at a time. I was there and observed the great efforts made by fire departments from the area. They came from the towns of Haileybury, New Liskeard, Latchford, Temagami, and as far away as Lorrain-ville and Ville Marie in Quebec. They fought very diligently, but against that wind not even the three water bombers which were sent in by the Ontario department of natural resources were able to help. The town lost about one quarter of its residences. There were 152 buildings burned. About 70 to 80 of these were dwellings, some multiple dwellings, which means that a very large part of the town has been destroyed.
It is almost impossible to imagine the kind of fire that we had in Cobalt. I have been through a number of fires, Mr. Speaker, and I have seen many forest fires, but I have never seen one of the intensity of this particular fire. The municipalities in the tri-town area met and offered assistance in the form of billets. Surprisingly 300 billets were available in the rest of Cobalt, 300 in Haileybury, and 300 in New Liskeard. Many larger towns would be proud of that kind of support. Interestingly enough, I sat in on council meeting the morning after the fire. The mayor had lost his home and was left with absolutely

nothing, apart from his clothes. Another councillor was in the same position. A third councillor saved his house which he recently built, but the house he lived in previously went up in flames. Three councillors, including the mayor, lost everything they owned.
The provincial government came through with help. The cabinet met and sent in two ministers who offered immediately half a million dollars and other assistance which would allow the town to raise money which would be matched by the province. I understand that the federal government was asked by my leader for unanimous consent to recognize that this was a tragedy regarding which everything possible should be done, but consent was not given. The former attorney general of Ontario did ask the Prime Minister a number of questions and, to summarize the Prime Minister said that everything possible would be done.
The other day I asked the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) if he would send in senior officials of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to sit down with the officials in Cobalt, the provincial officials and others to help iron out the difficulties, because the people want to rebuild Cobalt-they want to rebuild the houses they have lost. The Postmaster General (Mr. Blais) has political responsibilities in that area, but he does not have ministerial responsibility for CMHC. I think it is unfortunate that politics should be played at a time like this.
I am well aware the Minister of State for Urban Affairs was still enjoying the fruits of efforts he had been making elsewhere in another field at that time. If he were to go to Cobalt to look at the situation, he would also be more interested in getting rid of the red tape. If we are going to rebuild Cobalt, all the help that is possible must be given to those people. They must be encouraged to rebuild and to make their lives as they were before.
It is necessary for us to cut through the red tape in the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and other federal departments, including National Defence, which may be able to play a role through the Emergency Measures Organization by providing temporary housing. If that is all that is required, surely we are not going to play politics with it. The Minister of State for Urban Affairs could well have taken a ride on the same airplane in order to have a look at the situation. He could have been accompanied by some of his officials so that red tape would not be the bane, as it has been in so many other tragedies which have occurred in this country.

The government makes decisions with political input, and it seems to me the minister responsible for that region is the obvious minister to deal with the people. subtopic: CANADIAN EXPORT DEVELOPMENT CORPORATION-REASON FOR REFUSAL TO CONFIRM TRANSAIR AS PRIME BIDDER FOR UNITED STATES AIR FORCE CONTRACT
CANADIAN EXPORT DEVELOPMENT CORPORATION-REASON FOR REFUSAL TO CONFIRM TRANSAIR AS PRIME BIDDER FOR UNITED STATES AIR FORCE CONTRACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon I posed a question to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) with regard to a bid that Transair had made for a contract with the United States Air Force to overhaul 97 Boeing 707 tankers over a three year period. This work would entail modifying the wing structures.
Since my question this afternoon to the Minister of Transport I have been informed that it is the Canadian Commercial Corporation which has refused to write a letter of endorsation for Transair which must accompany the bid to the U.S. Air Force. There is still time for the CCC to give written confirmation that Transair is a prime bidder for the $42 million contract as bids do not close until July 1, 1977. I hope that the parliamentary secretary to the minister will get on to this tomorrow morning first thing and will have this letter of confirmation transferred to Transair so that they can apply for this bid, as the signing of the contract is to take place on July 1, 1977.
The first plane is to be delivered for overhaul on September 15, 1977. U.S. Air Force officials visited Winnipeg around
Adjournment Debate
November 1, 1976, and approved the new $15 million Air Canada hangar as the proper facility to do the overhauls. They have all the facilities to handle the overhaul contract for U.S. planes.
This afternoon when I raised my question I received a very unsatisfactory answer from the Minister of Transport who said "Essentially, my understanding from conversations with Transair is that the difficulty which had existed in connection with this bid, which may have prevented the bid from being successful, will not be repeated in the course of successive bids."
We do not get $42 million opportunities for Canada every day. Transair is the only company in Canada that has submitted a bid, and the U.S. Air Force is looking seriously at this contract submitted to Transair in Winnipeg. We want to remove the roadblocks, never mind putting road blocks in front of Transair. We have record unemployment in this country, we have economic chaos. Remove the road blocks, have this letter submitted to Transair tomorrow, and let us get this $42 million into Canada.
I received also another mundane, secondary answer from the Minister of Transport when he said this afternoon, "My understanding is that there may not be possibility of a bid in relation to those particular aircraft, but there are many hundreds of others which will be coming along next."
There are no $42 million contracts coming daily. They only come once in a lifetime. I have been informed tonight that the Canadian Commercial Corporation which will not submit this letter to Transair, has stated that it is incapable of handling this bid. This bid is only to rebuild the wing structure of the 97 planes. In the past Transair has completely rebuilt the Canadian 707s from top to bottom-it was not only the wing structure but the engines and everything else. Therefore this is nothing but a phony report from the CCC which says it will not submit this letter.
This has a two-fold impact on the Canadian economy. On May 23, 1974, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) made a flying trip to Winnipeg at which time he said he would give us a $15 million hangar. In the meantime we have embarrassed the Prime Minister into building this $15 million hangar for Air Canada, but Air Canada says it does not want it, it has no requirement for it. However, it is being built with federal funds and paid for by the Canadian taxpayer. Air Canada, I repeat, has stated that it does not need this hangar, and it does not know what to do with it. If this contract to overhaul these American air force 707 tankers comes into Canada, the work will be done in this new $15 million hangar, and Air Canada personnel will be involved in working on this particular contract, so it is particularly important that we do everything we possibly can to get this contract into Canada. Otherwise we would have this $15 million hangar just sitting there. It would just be an absolute and complete white elephant, so we have a two-fold impact here.
It has been stated earlier that with this $15 million hangar Transair will start doing some work, and it will lease part of the hangar facilities, but there is to be a merger of Transair with Pacific Western Airlines. If this merger is completed,

May 26, 1977
Adjournment Debate
there would be no more overhaul work done in Winnipeg. All the Transair and PWA overhaul work would be done in British Columbia and Alberta where their overhaul facilities are now. They would not be doing any work at all in this new $15 million hangar, so it is obvious that we must make every effort to assist Transair to obtain this contract with the American air force. Otherwise Canada will lose $42 million and 500 jobs.
It would require 500 people to overhaul the American air force planes over a three year period, and there is a possibility of other contracts later. If we lose this contract, we lose $42 million and 500 jobs, and we would be stuck with this huge monstrosity which the Prime Minister said in an election promise that he would build for us. We must make sure that this facility is used. We must make every effort to assist Transair to obtain this $42 million contract.

speakeroldname: Mr. Maurice A. Dionne (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: CANADIAN EXPORT DEVELOPMENT CORPORATION-REASON FOR REFUSAL TO CONFIRM TRANSAIR AS PRIME BIDDER FOR UNITED STATES AIR FORCE CONTRACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the Canada-U.S. defence production sharing arrangements entered into in 1956, the U.S. Department of Defence requires that generally, all purchases in excess of $10,000 from Canadian suppliers, shall be made with the Canadian Commercial Corporation. In order for Canadian contractors' bids to be considered for contract award by the U.S. defence department, CCC is required to give its endorsement on each bid submitted. This endorsement by CCC is, in effect, a guarantee to the U.S. government that all commitments and obligations of the bid and any resulting contract will be met. To determine if any bid will be endorsed, CCC, through its products centres, examines both the bid and the contractor to ensure that the financial, management and technical capability exists to perform the required work.
If a Canadian bid is selected by the U.S. for contract award, the contract is then made with CCC, which in turn sub-contracts 100 per cent to the Canadian supplier.
In response to a U.S. Air Force request for proposal, Transair Ltd. prepared a bid for the replacement of the lower wing skins of KC-135 aerial refueling tanker aircraft for the USAF. The work was to be a three year project involving some 97 aircraft, with further options of 36 aircraft in each of the following two years.
The company's response was sent direct to Tinker Air Force Base at Oklahoma City; a copy of the bid was also sent to CCC. In order for CCC to consider the Transair bid for endorsement, the company was asked to provide the corporation with comprehensive evidence of its capabilities in terms of facilities, manpower and technical skills and necessary financing.
The company had arranged to rent a hangar from Air Canada and had requested support from the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce on tooling. The basis of costing estimates was examined and judged to be reasonable. On March 31, 1977 Transair informed CCC of last minute difficulties in presenting satisfactory evidence of availability of working capital. As the bid closed the next day, it was certified to the U.S. Air Force subject only to determination that

adequate management, financing and physical facilities were available to perform the work.
The U.S. Air Force advised CCC on April 5 that the Transair proposal was found to be non-responsive and could not be accepted for further evaluation because of information contained in the Transair bid and CCC's partial endorsement.
Although in this case the bid was not accepted by the U.S. Department of Defense, the Canadian Commercial Corporation has, in the fiscal year 1976-77, received contract awards from the U.S. defense department totalling in excess of $100 million.

subtopic: HEALTH-POSSIBILITY OF STUDIES ON EFFECTS OF SACCHARIN ON HUMANS-REASON FOR FAILURE TO CONSULT MEDICAL ASSOCIATIONS PRIOR TO IMPOSING BAN
HEALTH-POSSIBILITY OF STUDIES ON EFFECTS OF SACCHARIN ON HUMANS-REASON FOR FAILURE TO CONSULT MEDICAL ASSOCIATIONS PRIOR TO IMPOSING BAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise tonight as a result of the rather inadequate and almost irrational response by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) as reported at page 4285 of Hansard for March 24, to a question I asked on the subject of saccharin. I asked the minister if he would indicate to the House what retrospective and prospective studies he has authorized or has done on the effect of saccharin on humans. I will quote the minister's reply in full. He said:
Mr. Speaker, decisions have been made in that field following studies which have been confirmed by international and American authorities. I would suggest to the hon. member that he not be overly impressed by a decidedly American lobbying organization which has more than $1 million at its disposal to rally public opinion against this decision.
I cannot see what that had to do with the question of studies of a retrospective and prospective nature regarding saccharin.
Before I continue my comments I would suggest to the parliamentary secretary who is here to answer for the minister that he lay aside the prepared speech given to him by his officials. I see he has a pen in his hand so I would encourage him to jot down the eight or ten questions I will ask so that he can reply briefly to them.
My questions will be in two parts. The first part will be a request for some indication of the policy of the department relating to decisions regarding research projects such as in saccharin, and the second part will inquire to what extent the department followed through on this policy.
My first question is what the policy of the department would be when dealing with research of this kind. Do they consult the Medical Research Council before they proceed and as they proceed with the program? In the case of saccharin did they consult with the Research Council before they initiated the project and as they proceeded?
My second question concerns the policy regarding research projects and the execution of retrospective studies. When checking food additives and so on, does the department have a policy of doing retrospective studies on human beings, no rats, when they have something of significance to contribute to the medical community? If so, what was done on human beings in respect of this particular experiment on rats?
May 26, 1977

My third question relates to prospective studies. Does the department have any policy regarding prospective studies in situations where they are studying a potentially harmful product consumed by humans? If so, have they initiated prospective studies on human beings in the use of saccharin? It should not be difficult to do for either prospective or retrospective studies. Certainly retrospective studies would be easy because saccharin has been used for 98 years and there are three or four generations that could be checked.
The fourth question refers to consultations. I am not sure the minister knows what a consultation is. I believe he thinks a consultation is a briefing. Before an announcement is made such as the one on saccharin, or previous ones on the swine 'flu virus vaccine or cyclamates, all of which have been catastrophic as far as the medical community is concerned, does the minister or his department make a point of engaging in consultation as opposed to briefing? I understand consultation did not happen. I ask, did they consult, not brief, professional associations like the CMA, the Canadian Dental Association and other, similar professional groups?
Fifth, and this question is also about consultation, is it the policy of the ministry to consult lay groups interested in that field? Specifically, did it consult with the Canadian Diabetic Association, the Canadian Cancer Society, the Canadian Heart Society, weight reducing organizations, and so on?
My sixth question is this: what is the minister's policy regarding consultations with manufacturing groups? Did he discuss saccharin with manufacturers of diet drinks, diet foods, and so on? Did he consult the grocery products manufacturers of Canada? That association ought to have been consulted. Did he consult the Calory Control Council of North America, which is interested in these matters?
Seventh, what is the government's policy on releasing partial information before all tests are completed? Almost two months after the minister banned saccharin, he announced that subsequent tests showed that the problem may have been caused by impurities in saccharin. I am referring to the Ames test.
Since the minister knew perfectly well that those tests had not been completed, why did he not wait two months before announcing the ban?
I direct three more general questions to the parliamentary secretary. First, I wish to quote part of the minister's reply to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) as reported on page 3836 of Hansard of March 10, 1977. Hansard reports the minister as saying in part:
We proposed the establishment of a committee, in co-operation with the industry and medical experts, to make a complete review of the role of saccharin in the diet of diabetics.
Has that been done?
Finally, since my time has almost run out, I make one last comment. The American Cancer Society publishes an excellent journal twice a month. In a recent article entitled, "The Environmental Time Bomb That Never Went Off' the editor
Adjournment Debate
of the journal, Arthur I. Holleb, wrote one particularly significant sentence, as follows:
Hasty judgments are a disservice to the serious study of environmental cancer.
I would welcome the parliamentary secretary's response to my questions.

speakeroldname: Mr. Paul E. McRae (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: HEALTH-POSSIBILITY OF STUDIES ON EFFECTS OF SACCHARIN ON HUMANS-REASON FOR FAILURE TO CONSULT MEDICAL ASSOCIATIONS PRIOR TO IMPOSING BAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I find it difficult at present to answer the hon. member's specific questions. The answers will have to be provided, for 1 cannot say who talked to whom in each case. I cannot answer the hon. member's eight or nine questions in three minutes. I point out that all hon. members have had the opportunity to be briefed. I think it would have been possible to raise these questions in the presence of officials responsible for the studies mentioned. I do not recall many questions having been asked when the opportunity for briefing arose.
The hon. member raised the question of the Medical Research Council. I would not venture to say yes or not to his questions. The information will have to be provided.
I must make a strong point on the question of retrospective and prospective studies. As the hon. member knows, it is not possible to use human subjects in the study of carcinogenic agents. It would be unethical to attempt to induce cancer of the bladder in a human being.
The other point is that saccharin has been used for 90 years, but used extensively only for the last eight years. In two cases there is evidence to suggest that saccharin may have caused cancer, although that is not positive.
I come to the question of consultation. The department has consulted with officials of CMA, the Canadian Diabetic Association and the Canadian Dental Association, but the department itself had to make a decision. Certainly there was a discussion with the industry, the bottling industry and groups like that.
With regard to testing for the possibility of impurities, there are two problems. First, it would have to be proven that the impurities were causing the trouble. Second, it would have to be proven that a form of saccharin could be formed which did not have those impurities or other carcinogenic impurities. It is a problem.
If we had said we were not going to do anything about it, the Canadian Medical Association and the opposition would be telling us to ban that particular substance from our foods. That would have been the case if we had found strong evidence that it produced carcinogenic results. The department acted right away. Some changes may have to be made. I cannot say whether consultation has started with the Canadian Diabetic Association. I hope it has. If not, as the minister indicated, I am sure it will in the near future.
